PRIORY 3x2.5m RELAY, REIGATE, 7 OCT It took Helen 16:29 to tour the testing hills of the Reigate Priory and she was just under a minute slower than the fastest time of the day for her 4th place on leg one. Nina Mills was next away, clocking 19:02 to bring the team in 9th, and a now constantly improving Jacqui Smiter enjoyed herself on the final leg, picking off two of the opposition with her 17:56 effort. This was good running from our ladies - 7th place out of the 20 teams that finished. 1, Croydon 47:38; 2, Cambridge H 50:58; 3, Herne Hill 51:13; ... 7, Belgrave 53:27. SURREY CC LEAGUE, DIV. 2 RACE 2, EWELL COURT, 28 NOV With Morag Andrew and Gabby Collison drafted into the team it became a fight to get into the scoring five and the overall result was a resounding win for the Bels. and a fine individual victory for Helen. This course might be normally classed as flat and grassy but heavy rain had turned parts of the circuit into a leg-sapping quagmire - and then there was the descent down the slippery banks and through the muddy waters of the River Hogsmill to contend with on each lap! Eventually it was the two 'Js' who filled out the score sheet, pushing Nina Mills back to become our 6th placer. But watch out for the young woman who was next home and making her debut in Belgrave colours. Martina Ryan is no stranger to cross-country, having run regularly as a junior back in Ireland. It shouldn't take her too long to run off the few intervening years of inactivity, particularly as the Ryan family are in residence at the 'King of Denmark'; how convenient for training from Belgrave Hall just around the corner. 1, H. Jacqui Smiter's hard winter's training is beginning to pay off but what can you say about Jacinta Moore - a baby due in three months time and here she was closing off the scoring team to ensure that the Bels. claimed 2nd team prizes. 1, G.Collison (Belgrave) 17:46; 2, H.Imeson (Tadworth) 18:46; 3, J.Whyte (Tadworth) 19:51; 4, J.Smiter 19:59; 7, J.Moore 21:03; 8, S.Porter 24:31. SURREY CC CHAMPS., COULSDON, 12 DEC Bright sunshine prevailed for the county championships but conditions were sticky underfoot and by the end of the afternoon it was pretty cold as well. The start entailed a swift couple of circuits around the field at Fox Common before the pack headed off down into Happy Valley with Woking's Zara Hyde making the running. Helen Maskrey was in the leading bunch of half a dozen and with Gabrielle Collison and Morag Andrew shoulder to shoulder close behind and only three to score, our hopes of getting into the medals looked good. Hyde proved to be in devastating form, getting right away from the field for a clear win, but the team race turned out to be a very close affair. Woking, of course, had a good start with the individual winner but while waiting for the rest of their squad, Croydon got two home with 4th and 6th and Herne Hill were also in the frame with 7th and 9th. Then, with Helen fighting up the final slope to spearhead our team with 11th place, chased by Woking's second scorer and Herne Hill's third, we saw Morag and Gabby appear at the top of the long drag up from the Valley in 14th and 17th places. Minds numbed from the cold found it too difficult to keep four lots of mental arithmetic going but with Croydon's last scorer still nowhere in sight we began to feel sure of bronze medals. But it was not to be so! Croydon had to wait until 30th place to get their last girl home but their early scorers were just too far up for us to counter. UK WORLD CC TRIALS, CORBY, 6 FEB For someone who hadn't really done any cross country before the start of this winter, Helen Maskrey has become involved in a big way. Her running in the County Championships earned her a Surrey vest and here she was along with the cream of the nation's distance runners competing in the trial for the International Champs. The race was won by Suzanne Rigg of Cheshire in 18:38 but Helen was well into the first half of the field, placing 130th of the 305 finishers, in 21:44. What a warm up for the following day's ... 26.2/SECURICOR 10k, Inc. SURREY CHAMPS, WEST EWELL, 7 FEB A huge field set out from Hook Arena on the 10k circuit that takes in Chessington, Malden Rushett and Epsom Common before returning to West Ewell. Some familiar faces were to be seen along the way, marking the course: Billy Bull and our Kingsmeadow gang, Leo Coy - even Sue Porter out doing some training. Your cycle-bourne reporter found it impossible to pick out all our ladies during the initial rush but did notice Jacqui Smiter and Martina Ryan in close company. Having let the field pass, some furious pedalling was necessary to work back towards the top of the pack. As the faster runners were picked up and the field became more spread out, there was still no sign of a Belgrave vest - maybe I had missed our top three. But no, the fact was that they were startlingly way up the field and as Chessington Zoo was neared, the slim frame of Gabby Collison could be seen bobbing along with her characteristic, easy style. A few more turns of the pedals and there were Morag and Helen, stride for stride with only Moyra Jordan of Horsham up ahead. My goodness, after last year's 2nd place, we were going to "walk" the team race with packing like this! Racing ahead to find a "photo spot", the runners were not seen again until they turned into Horton Lane with nearly 2 miles to go. It was Morag who appeared first, running fiercely with Helen some 20 metres in arrears. An International runner for Scotland a few years back, Morag has had a couple of years out of the sport during which time she has started a family but now she shows all the signs of edging back to some good class running again. On to the finish. Jordan was first through the gates and onto the grassy finishing area but before she had crossed beneath the final banner a girl in claret and gold had also turned onto the straight. It was Helen. Somewhere along that final long road she had got ahead of her rival - but only just, because a mere three seconds separated them. Second and third, and now here was Gabby, all three of our scorers on the finish straight at the same time. Further down the field more fine running was evident. Jacqui had smashed her pb and Martina had made a fine first appearance on the road in Belgrave colours. Of course we did win the team race and when it came to the County Championship we had the perfect score of 6 points for 1st, 2nd and 3rd. Apparently this has never been done before in a Senior Surrey championship. 1, M.Jordan (Horsham) 36:11; 2, H.Maskrey (Belgrave) 36:27; 3, M.Andrew (Belgrave) 36:30; 4, G.Collison 36:51; ... J.Smiter, M.Ryan, S.Howard also ran but further details not known. Teams: 1, Belgrave. Surrey Champs: 1, Belgrave. SURREY CC LEAGUE, DIV. 2 RACE 4, LLOYD PARK 13 MAR What a contrast to the day of the men's league race in early January. Then the course had been a morass and spirits were as low as the heavy grey clouds, with the Bels. due to suffer another hammering. But come the spring and the women's race, we had a firm, dry, grassy course (albeit a little rutted), beautiful blue skies, a picnic atmosphere and the certain prospect of promotion to division one. After the very first kilometre there were a few surprises to note. Morag Andrew had made a determined start and was clearly placed ahead of our normal team leader, Helen Maskrey. Gabby Collison was close behind and then came Martina Ryan, already away from Jacqui Smiter for the first time in the series and moving strongly. These positions were not to change throughout the duration of the surely over-length race. Helen did not seem unduly worried by playing second fiddle for a change and one got the impression that the following day's Belgrave Half-Marathon was on her mind. Poor Jacqui was struggling though, troubled by stomach cramps that made a fight with Martina impossible. But there was no doubt at all that the latter was having a brilliant race and, the possessor a good "running" brain, we can look for a lot more to come from her yet. The past few weeks had seen her ease off from the Club-night runs with the men, with a switch of emphasis to sustained, fast, shorter runs on the grass of the Common. Well done Martina! Just outside the scoring five Jacinta Moore made a welcome return to the team. Incredible though it may seem, she had been due to give birth on just about the date of this race, but baby Cliona had conveniently seen fit to enter the world a month early, leaving Jacinta to gradually get back into her running, avoiding the cold days and taking it as it comes. Once again young Laura Wilson flew the flag for Belgrave in the minors' event with a very strong race for 4th place. Veterans' Results SURREY COUNTY VETERANS CC CHAMPS., RICHMOND PARK, 17 OCT In the middle of one of the wettest Autumns in memory, the Surrey Vets Cross Country Championships managed as usual to pick a bright, sunny afternoon, although a stiff breeze chilled the runners especially as they ran past the lake. There was a good turn out of 18 from Belgrave, including two ladies, in a field of 120 runners and there was a welcome first appearance for the "newly turned forty" Mike Gleave. At the front the race was dominated by Thames Hare and Hounds with Dave Hill winning as he pleased and Mike Farmery, another new Vet, coming through strongly for second ahead of Chris Hughes and a tired Charlie Dickinson. Rex Bale ran well to finish in the first thirty with Alan Painter completing the scoring three. The Belgrave fifties team were rather unfortunate not to get a medal. Tony Stone limped out of the race with a pulled a hamstring at the end of the first lap which left Tony Hardy to lead in a scoring three made up by John Wasbrough and Mike Newton. It was nice to see Mike racing for the first time since his eye operation in the summer. The race organisers, Ranelagh, were awarding an over sixties team category for the first time and the rampant Belgrave trio of Pat Newell, Bert Stroud and Charlie Walker came away with the team gold scoring the minimum of six points. The M60 race was won by Jim Chandler of Waverley but close behind there was a right ding dong between the three Belgrave runners. Eventually a rather out of sorts Charlie Walker was dropped by the in form Bert Stroud, with Pat Newell tucked in behind. At the finish a very fit and determined Pat just got the better of Bert to take individual silver. Another triumph for our over sixties team! CAMBRIDGE H VETERANS RELAYS, ROCHESTER, 20 DEC The Belgrave over 50 team made their annual successful Christmas pilgrimage to Rochester for the 4x2.6m road relay around the aerodrome, although they found the opposition rather tougher this year. These relays are becoming increasingly popular, with teams from Swindon, Aldershot and Woodford Green supplementing the usual Kent based contingent. The event, organised by David Coward, is sponsored by a local butcher and there is much meat given out at the end in the way of prizes. Perhaps Belgrave were a little lucky to collect their joints of pork. We finished fourth but as the third team were Cambridge "B", the Bels. were deemed the third club to finish. It's all very friendly. Best run of the day was again from Tony Verdie who seems to like this event. He completed the second fastest lap in 13:51 to Davidson's 13:39. Having done his usual Potteries Marathon in October, Tony finds this event far enough away from his next major marathon, usually the London, to risk testing his speed. Well Tony, the speed is obviously still there, pity we can't get you onto the track! VETERANS AC CC CHAMPS, WIMBLEDON, 23 JAN No less than eleven Belgravians preferred to run in the VAC Championships rather than the Club '10' held on the same day, at the same time, and over roughly the same course. The VAC Championships are always well organised, with trophies and medals in five year age groups, very competitive, with the course demanding but of a reasonable length. The Vet in form is Bob Treadwell, a full minute ahead of Tony Simmonds in the home international at Belfast, Surrey Senior Champion at Coulsdon in December, and 23rd in the South of England. When he arrived at the start the result was a foregone conclusion. It is interesting that the quality at the "sharp end" now rivals the Southern Vets Championships. The depth has been there for some years but now VAC are beginning to pick up more members from, for example, Kent and North London. It was Grenville Tuck who led the leading bunch over the golf course and down through the woods with Charlie Dickinson starting more cautiously in sixth place. Both came unstuck in the mud through the fields at the bottom where Treadwell began to force the pace ahead of Morten and Daniel of Blackheath. Charlie moved up to third on the horse ride and chased hard, but Treadwell moved steadily away on lap two and the very strong Hugh Morten maintained the gap for 2nd. Treadwell broke the course record set last year by Terry Osbourne and said afterwards that without the Southern in his legs from the week before, and on firmer ground he might have been close to 24 minutes! His elder brother John, a regular and popular member of VAC, took the M45 trophy. Nor did the wet conditions stop Maggie Statham from breaking the W35 record again or our own Laurie O'Hara from bringing the M60 record down to an amazing 28:16. The quality of the M60's was such that Bert Stroud, Charlie Walker and Pat Newell all missed medals in spite of excellent runs. Bert was just beaten to the line by Thomas of Cambridge. SOUTHERN VETS CC CHAMPS., LLOYD PARK, 5 FEB This event has become less popular with Belgrave Vets over the last couple of years and the only one to brave the sticky mud and the hills of Lloyd Park was ... yes, you've guessed it, Charlie Walker. Charlie ran very well, winning the bronze medal in the M60 race. He might have done even better had he not run off course when leading at the end of the second of the three lap course. He was running just behind the pack of leading Lady Vets and hadn't realised that they had turned off for their finish. Charlie lost a good forty or fifty metres and the lead. Should have kept your eyes on the course Charlie! M60: 1, M.Baker (Horsham) 42:49; 2, D.Thomas (Cambridge H) 42:51; 3, C.Walker (Belgrave)43:56. BVAF NATIONAL CC CHAMPS., BURNLEY, 7 MAR It was an early Sunday morning start for the combined Belgrave/VAC party who made the long trip north to Burnley for this year's Vets National. A successful trip too, with Bob Treadwell winning the M40 race, silver medals for the Belgrave M60 team, and Bob Belmore a rival member of the winning Barnet squad. On arrival, Townley Park fell somewhat short of the vision some had of beautiful north country moors. The start was a flat scrubby playing field alongside a dirty stream, then came a long, long, muddy climb of at least three quarters of a mile up to the edge of a council estate at the top of the surrounding hills. Down again, past a huge ugly factory, and then came the wade through a smelly stream to the finish. All this three times. However, the day was very well organised, the competition intense, and one wise old runner kindly reminded us that when the race was last held in the South the venue was Wormwood Scrubs! With Laurie O'Hara missing from the Belgrave team it was Charlie Walker, in inspired form, who led the Belgrave M60's in the first race. Charlie finished 7th in his age category, an improvement from last year and even ahead of a tired looking Tony Stone. Strong runs from Bert Stroud and Pat Newell made up the scoring three with Arthur Bruce and Fred Paget freely offering advice from the side. Barnet had their new star, Ron Higgs, and did just enough to take gold, which of course was much commented upon afterwards by Bob Belmore. Bob Treadwell had rested from the National at Parliament Hill the previous week in anticipation of the strong field and the demanding course. He found the long, slow climbs to his liking, reminiscent of several Continental hill races that had given him success in the past and suited to long striding runners with long hamstrings who are able to find the right breathing rhythm. (All age winners were built thus.) Bob got away on the first climb, and although always wary of the in form Brian Kirkwood from Scotland who finished ahead of him in the Inter-Counties, held on well for a great victory. Charlie Dickinson hasn't got long hamstrings and was rather disappointed with 26th place after finishing 11th the previous year. The long drive as chauffeur may also have taken its toll. With Maggie Statham, coached by Bob Belmore, and Steve Charlton also winning their races, it was a successful day for VAC and the South. The long drive home gave us a mixture of snoozing, stories of races from the past and more friendly Belgrave/Barnet banter. "Don't worry, we'll have you lot in the relay". "Why don't you rejoin us instead of running for that North London lot ? On second thoughts it would be a waste of time, we don't run a 'B' team !" Well, perhaps not quite so friendly ! items.sum: Leo Coy reviews the young athletes' cross-country season and their first year in the U13 Indoor Sportshall League.
items.s: Another successful season Leo Coy reviews the young athletes' cross-country season and their first year in the U13 Indoor Sportshall League. Another successful season Another successful cross-country season has ended with good all round performances by all age group teams and some very good individual results. The season got under way in October with a win for the Youths in the Surrey CC Relay. The event was held on the old Surrey AC relay course in Richmond Park. Our HHH League performance was probably our best ever. We managed to get team or individual prizes in all groups as well as winning third overall for combined age groups. Simon Vella, Gavin Jones, John Wilson and Adam Jones all performed very well in each match. In the Surrey League our combined Youths/Boys team had no opposition all year. Matthew Hillier won two races with Adam Jones and Gavin Mason winning the other two. This, with good back-up from the Boys, ensured that we won with ease. Tom Evans and Simon Alexander had great runs at Lloyd Park - they surprised some of the Youths and pushed them out of the scoring five! Unfortunately we will be in Division Two with the Seniors next year. The County Championships saw mixed performances with the best result coming from Simon Vella, who came 2nd in the Middlesex Colts' race. At the Southern, we finished our full quota of eight in the Boys' age group and the team were 20th. Simon Alexander had a good run to lead the team home in 51st place. The Youths team finished 7th overall, without Gavin or Stuart Booth. Matthew and Adam had excellent runs. This year for the first time we participated in the Indoor Sportshall League for the U13 age group. The league was held over three matches and took place in large sports halls. The events consist of sprints, relays, paarlauf, plus throws and jumps. Each team is made up of six competitors and each can only do one individual event. Everybody takes part in the final relay. The competition was fierce, with an excellent atmosphere at each venue. It is an exciting event which will continue to grow in popularity and will be an alternative to an easy winter for our young throwers, sprinters and jumpers. We performed well throughout and won the final match at Cheam. Es Hassan, Andrew Hill, Duncan Thompson, Steve Taylor and Dwaine Patterson were selected to represent Surrey in the National Event. Thanks to Chris. Knight, Billy Bull and Martin Milner for their help throughout the season and also thanks to the parents who supported us so well. I must not forget Steve Whorlow, for his role as acting team manager when I was delayed - I did have a long way to travel. Captains Toby, Marlon and Adam played their part all season during both training and competition. Next season sees the start of the new age bands which will mean that most of our Youths will miss their second winter season in the age group and will become Juniors. Let us hope that they continue to improve together and become our Senior team of the future. items.h: Step by step guide to Athletic Meetings
items.sum: Sue Porter describes how track and field officials get involved and what organising an athletics meeting involves, appealing for helpers.
items.s: Step by step guide to Athletic Meetings Sue Porter describes how track and field officials get involved and what organising an athletics meeting involves, appealing for helpers. Step by step guide to Athletic Meetings Everyone competes at athletic meetings, local leagues or national leagues and probably only notice the field and track officials in passing. They're those men and women in the navy jackets! How do these officials get involved in the first place? Often it's as a parent helping out, holding tapes, collecting shot, even timekeeping. Then before they know it they're hooked and, having taken a straightforward test, become a Graded Official, the first step on the ladder to becoming Chief Track Judge, Referee or Timekeeper. So now we have a band of officials, how do we proceed? We first have to agree on a date to hold the meeting. This is a lot more difficult than you would expect or believe. With so many meetings held in the summer, tracks are booked up very early. And of course it's best not to clash with national or county events, or any of the established leagues. Once the date has been sorted out then a timetable and list of events can be drawn up. Adverts for entries are placed in the magazines and circularised to other clubs in the area and then it's time to sit back and wait for the entries to come pouring in. On the day itself, the most important concern is the weather. As long as the rain isn't too heavy, or the snow can be swept off the track and field areas, we are all systems go. Also, whether or not all officials and helpers manage to park their cars close enough to the track to haul their bags of wet gear and other equipment; and whether the refreshments are available throughout the meeting. Officials work best on sweet tea and ginger biscuits. After a successful meeting you'd think it would be an easy matter to lock up and return all the equipment to the rightful places. But there's always some items of kit to return to owners - if you can find them. One starter, who shall remain nameless, was without his red jacket - heaven forbid - for some months. Don't ask how he managed to be an official starter without it. So then it's time to retire, battered and shattered and mentally bereft, to go through the results and send out the medals, etc., not collected. Oh well! Leave that 'til tomorrow ... Tomorrow's another day - and next week's another meeting ... Easy isn't it? You too can help, you really can. You're only a 'phone call away from a fun-filled summer officiating for Belgrave Harriers. Sue Porter (Club Starter & General Secretary) Sue Porter Sue Porter Club Starter and General Secretary

items.sum: Harry Porter's profile of Ladies' Captain Jacinta Moore (née Coppinger): her running since joining from Dublin in 1985, her GRE Cup 3,000m win at Kingston in 1987, her marriage and the birth of daughter Cliona.
items.s: A Team Manager's DREAM Harry Porter's profile of Ladies' Captain Jacinta Moore (née Coppinger): her running since joining from Dublin in 1985, her GRE Cup 3,000m win at Kingston in 1987, her marriage and the birth of daughter Cliona. Harry Porter writes about Jacinta Moore née Coppinger, one of our Ladies' Captains, whom he describes as A Team Manager's DREAM I first met Jacinta in November 1985, just after the cross-country season had started. It was my second season as Ladies Team Manager, having succeeded Derek Jones after his five year stint. Since that time Jacinta has competed on the Road, Country and Track, making over 150 appearances in the Belgrave team despite a break of some months due to muscle injury and extensive physiotherapy. Jacinta's first appearance for Belgrave was at the Surrey Women's Cross Country League Meeting at Ewell Court, just before Christmas 1985. She had only recently come to England from her native Dublin and had joined us soon after her arrival. That first season started with a good first run, 23rd, and she went on to finish the winter in 13th. Not bad at all for a first attempt. She had originally wanted to run longer distances and even now enjoys an occasional half-marathon. In fact she came second to Leslie Watson in the Welwyn 20 mile road race in February 1985 and in 1990 ran alongside the likes of Greta Weitz and Rosa Mota in the Women's Great London Run over 10k where she finished a creditable 21st in 38:34. That 10k was a pretty good performance when you consider that the day before she had run in the Hertford County Road Relays where her second-claim team had placed 2nd. Representing Hertfordshire on numerous occasions over both Country and Track, Jacinta's best result was a fourth position in the County Cross Country Championships of 1988 and she has run for that county in the Southern and National Inter-Counties events. On the track she was silver medallist in the Herts. County Championships 3,000m for two consecutive years from 1988, running 10:40 both times. Having lived in Surrey for the last two years, Jacinta now has Surrey qualifications and in 1992 ran the in the County 10k Road Championships when the Belgrave Ladies were second team. The team went on to win the first ever Women's Surrey Road League in the summer of 1992. As well as track and cross-country, Jacinta also enjoys the longer relays, and in particular the now defunct 25 x 1 mile relay held at the end of the track season. She competed in the race every year until the last in 1989. However, since 1988 the Ladies have also taken part in the Ostende Relays. The distances in this event vary from 100m to 600m and Jacinta has run a 600m leg ever since the team first ventured onto the Continent. She was also a member of the Southern Women's 3 x 800m gold medal winning team in 1987, along with Jacqui Smiter and Jackie Stone. Jacinta has been Track Captain since 1986 when she saw the team finish 7th in their first season in the Southern Women's League Division 2, narrowly missing promotion direct to Division 1. And in 1987 she led Belgrave into the semi-final of the GRE Cup, the only Division 2 team to have achieved that status since 1984. Jacinta considers that her most memorable day was the Melbourne Trophy International match at Crystal Palace in September 1987, where she came 3rd in the mile in 5:16.86. However, I would have to disagree, remembering her 4th place in the Surrey Women's Cross Country League match at Ewell Court, November 1990. But then again, from the spectators point of view, her 3,000m in that GRE Cup semi-final qualifier at Kingston in June 1987 takes some beating. She had gone out hard in front, leading the race for the first three laps. The rest of the pack, after recovering from the shock, gradually managed to pull her back and the Belgravian dropped to 4th position, to all intents and purposes, spent. But not so, because 400 metres from the finish she changed gear and went for the front again, making up over 30 metres in the last lap. To roaring and screaming from Belgrave teammates she surged through at the line to finish 1st. The whole field crossed the line within 5 metres. It was a thrilling race and she had gained six valuable points which took the team into the semi-finals for 1987. Jacinta had knocked a massive 1 minute off her personal best at the beginning of that season and a further 13 seconds had come off just two weeks previously. What a tremendous performance and what a memorable day for the whole team. Apart from having competed for Belgrave and Hertfordshire, Jacinta also enters many road races, both here and in Eire. In 1991 she won the Limerick 5 miles road title, and she also took the Billericay 9 miles with 57:20. However, life changed drastically and irrevocably for Jacinta in that year. She met her future husband Michael after an unfortunate accident with wet paint - you will have to ask Jacinta for the full story - my lips are sealed. But the incident did prove very fortunate for the couple who married towards the end of 1991, when Sue and myself were privileged to attend on behalf of the Club. The wedding was held on a beautiful sunny day at a quiet country church beside the shimmering waters of a lough. At a photocall afterwards, the neat group of Michael, his parents and two brothers were swamped when the photographer innocently called for the bride and her family. Jacinta's parents, her eleven brothers and sisters and their wives and children surged into view - the photographer needed a wide angle lens to cope with this sitting! "It was a quiet year," says Jacinta. In June 1992 Jacinta spread the glad tidings that she was pregnant, and her daughter Cliona was born on 1st February this year. Jacinta had raced in the Wimbledon 5k in early December, just eight weeks before the baby's arrival, and was back in action in the very last cross-country race of the season, which included the Belgrave Championships, on March 13th. Almost a Liz McColgan! Many team managers would dream of having a Jacinta in their team. She is wholly committed to her club where, for her, events takes precedence over any other competition. She is one of those rare people who are able to get that little bit extra from people when that little bit extra can make all the difference. A good motivator without a doubt, the Belgrave Women's Section is so much the better for her presence. For everything you have achieved for us, Jacinta, we all thank you. Well done - and here's to the future too. Harry Porter Left: With 300m to go in the 1992 Club Championship 800m Jacinta Moore was still shadowed by Jackie Stone but by the end of the back stretch Jacinta was away for a comfortable win. items.sum: Ladies Team Manager Harry Porter congratulates the women on their winter season, including the Surrey League Division 2 title and Surrey road championship trophies.
items.s: Thanks from Harry P Ladies Team Manager Harry Porter congratulates the women on their winter season, including the Surrey League Division 2 title and Surrey road championship trophies. Thanks from Harry P As Ladies Team Manager, I would like to congratulate the Ladies for their very successful season over the country and road this winter, following their achievement in winning the first Surrey Women's Summer Road League in 1992. Over the winter of 1992/93 the women turned in tremendous performances to win the Surrey Cross Country League Division 2 by a huge margin and gain promotion to Division 1. Although down on numbers for the Winter Road League, they still managed to come a creditable 3rd. In the 5k and 10k Surrey Road Championships our Ladies took both trophies and in the longer race we won with the minimum score - our team placing 1st, 2nd and 3rd in the Surrey race and 2nd, 3rd and 4th overall. Many congratulations. Well done! Let's hope that this sparkling winter can transfer onto the track for equally good performances in the Southern Women's T&F League and Surrey Summer Road League. As well as the good performances, I would like to thank my Assistant Team Manager, Cynthia James, and travelling official, Derek Jones, for their sterling efforts on our behalf. items.s: A little depleted Carl Lawton's walking section round-up of a thin winter, with walkers away, injured or off form, and news of a vets' track league and a possible ladies team. A little depleted The winter season did not produce much in the way of success. We still rely on the mature walkers and with the absence of Doug Fotheringham and John Dunsford on a three month jaunt to foreign parts and competing in the Oceanic Games, we have been a little depleted. To add to our woe Paul King had a disagreement with a car (who said "Not again!") so he has been off the road since January. Pat Duncan achieved a performance that has taken him 30 years - he actually beat Ray Middleton in a race. However, Ray will probably admit to being a little off form. During the next few months there is the chance to join in with the track and field side competing in the vets. league over 2k. Those interested please see fixture card. It is only two over 40s and one over 50 to score but there will be space for non-scorers. Karen Barker has been off the road for a while but now having given birth to twins, both girls, she may soon be out and about again. To give her some incentive Gill Brackpool has started training again and so there is the possibility of having a ladies team out. items.sum: Belgrave race walking reports and results from September 1992 to April 1993, from the London Postal Region 10k to the Southern RWA & London and Sussex, Surrey & Kent, Middlesex and National and Southern 20k Championships, with wins by Carl Lawton, John Hall and Paul King, a guest win by Simon Baker in the club 3k, and a page of Heather Miller's photos from the Belgrave Open '7'.
items.s: Walking Belgrave race walking reports and results from September 1992 to April 1993, from the London Postal Region 10k to the Southern RWA & London and Sussex, Surrey & Kent, Middlesex and National and Southern 20k Championships, with wins by Carl Lawton, John Hall and Paul King, a guest win by Simon Baker in the club 3k, and a page of Heather Miller's photos from the Belgrave Open '7'. LONDON POSTAL REGION 10k, BLACKHEATH, 6 SEP Lawton was in the frame as the Bels. backed him up to a rare team triumph. Mike Scamell was in particular having a good month, and able to break the paternal pattern now required of Mike the 'Dad.' 1, S.Davis (Ilford) 48:36; 2, G.Hunwicks (Wey) 48:56; 3, C.Lawton (Belgrave) 50:19; ... 7, M.Scamell 53:23; 9, P.Warburton 54:58; 14, P.King 55:56; 15, D.Fotheringham 56:08. Teams: 1, Belgrave 19; 2, Medway 28. BELGRAVE 3k TRACK CHAMPS, BATTERSEA PARK, 7 SEP The following day, on a nearly deserted Battersea track, a World and Commonwealth Champion had a spin in Bels. colours and duly won the race if not the Club Championship. Simon Baker, about to return to Oz, two hours later in fact, was staying with Paul Warburton who strong-armed the Victorian into his first effort since the Olympic 50k! 1, S.Baker (Australia) 13:10.3; 2, C.Cheeseman (Surrey WC) 13:43.2; 5, P.Warburton 15:33.2; 6, D.Fotheringham 16:05.3. CIVIL SERVICE 7m, BLACKHEATH, 9 SEP Back to Blackheath for another Bels. win; this time in the form of John Hall in his Min of Ag. colours, making light of the undulating course. He was followed by the rarely seen shape of John Llewellin, now working in deepest Kent. 1, J.Hall 54:08; ... 3, J.Llewellin 55:??. BERT ANGELL 7m, HENDON, 13 SEP Bels. on a roll decided to cash in at Hendon where Lawton was at the finish long before his team mates Scamell and Warburton who nonetheless had better than average efforts. 1, C.Lawton (Belgrave) 53:28; 2, S.Uttley (Ilford) 54:33; 3, M.Scamell (Belgrave) 54:38; ... 5, P.Warburton 57:17; 6, R.Middleton 60:41. BELGRAVE OPEN 5m, WIMBLEDON, 3 OCT This must have been the smallest ever field for this event and unless numbers generally increase must spell the end. 1, D.Baxter (Steyning) 40:55; 2, C.Lawton (Belgrave) 43:20; 3, D.Fotheringham 44:22; 4, P.King 45:30; 8 finished. CAMBRIDGE H WINTER LEAGUE 10k, BEXLEY, 24 OCT Excuse No. 63! the 'off' found at least four of the field tying up their laces. Reason? The gun at these races is synchronised with two other 'starts': when these go - everyone does, regardless of previously announced start times. Needless to say, two of the tardy had mixed fortunes. Paul Warburton called it quits trying to make up lost ground, while Surrey's Chris Cheeseman passed the entire field bar one: the organiser, Noel Carmody. (Are you trying to say something, Ed.?) 1, N.Carmody (Cambridge H) 46:54; 2, C.Cheeseman (Surrey WC) 47:12; 3, S.Uttley (Ilford) 49:47; ... 7, D.Fotheringham 55:03; 8, P.King 56:13. ENFIELD OPEN 7m, 14 NOV This course, over the years, has decreased in scope while traffic on the surrounding roads of the Q.E. Stadium has grown, which while making for a traffic free environment, now presents new hazards: footballs and toddlers; the former flying off the adjacent pitches, the latter let off the leash by unsuspecting parents - into the path of 8 mile an hour walkers. Not that this made any difference to Steyning's Darrell Stone, or for that matter to a relatively replete Belgrave team, who did well to finish in the frame, and avoid obstacles! 1, D.Stone (Steyning) 48:56; 2, J.Ball (Steyning) 50:58; 3, C.Cheeseman (Surrey WC) 51:57; ... 5, J.Hall 55:20; 11, C.Lawton 57:24; 17, P.Warburton 60:40; 19, M.Scamell 60:55; 23, D.Fotheringham 63:01; 24, P.King 63:09; 33, J.Dunsford 66:17. Teams: 1, Steyning 18; 2, Surrey WC 51; 3, Belgrave 52. HEWITT TROPHY 10k, BRIGHTON, 21 NOV Held on the road to the west and high above the Brighton track on a dull and foggy day, a Belgrave winner evolved; not in the fastest time but as nearest finishing time to that estimated. Paul King was in fact spot on, and this after arriving late and being coerced into changing. 1, P.King (Brighton) 47:25; ... 7, C.Lawton 50:40; 12, P.Warburton 53:40; 16, P.King 56:10; 19, P.Duncan 58:13. BELGRAVE OPEN 7m, WIMBLEDON, 28 NOV Almost another walking milestone! Lisa Langford won the Ilford inter-club a few years ago, beating John Hall. The Belgrave '7' almost repeated the performance only this time it was Julie Drake and John Hall. John, probably not having forgotten the previous occasion, put all his effort in to hold off Julie and break away for a clear win. The turn-out was slightly down on last year and only three teams closed in, thus giving Basingstoke a place in the frame. Men 1, J.Hall (Belgrave) 53:44; 2, P.Hannell (Surrey WC) 55:01; 3, S.Maidment (Steyning) 55:19; ... 5, C.Lawton 56:23; 10, P.Warburton 58:44; 16, P.King 60:53; 22, P.Duncan 63:53. Teams: 1, Surrey WC 27; 2, Belgrave 32; 3, Basingstoke 145. Women 1, J.Drake (Brighton) 54:26. MET. POLICE 11k, IMBER COURT, 10 JAN A cold miserable day and under 50 finishers. Belgrave could only manage 4th due to some sub-par performances. 1, J.Ball (Steyning) 50:35; 2, C.Cheeseman (Surrey) 51:33; 3, N.Carmody (Cambridge H) 52:42; ... 7, J.Hall 55:58; 15, P.Warburton 58:56; 18, C.Lawton 59:55; 29, P.Duncan 64:39. Teams: 1, Steyning 21; 2, Surrey 32; 3, Ilford 50; 4, Belgrave 58. BELGRAVE INTER-CLUB 10m, WIMBLEDON, 23 JAN Not content with finishing 2nd in the Belgrave '7', Julie Drake came back for more and won this event. But Belgrave's turn-out was rather depleted. 1. D.Baxter (Steyning) 1:21:10; 2, J.Hall (Belgrave) 1:22:51; 3, S.Lightman (Surrey) 1:24:29; ... 12, P.Duncan 1:39:56. Teams: 1, Surrey 13; 2, London Vidarians 42. SOUTHERN RWA & LONDON CHAMPS, CRYSTAL PALACE, 6 FEB Poor John Keown! The Belgrave stalwart and sometime Southern Area Secretary was led a merry dance by the Sports Council who promised financial returns in exchange for the championships being shifted from the traditional venue of Battersea Park to the park paths surrounding the National Sporting Centre. Not only did the money never appear, but John and Mick and Barbara Marshall had to battle all kinds of bureaucratic blunders to get the races staged at all. Nor did the date appeal to some. At least one south coast club whose fixture had always been on the first Saturday in February, complained bitterly in print about the choice of this date for the championships, which now incorporate three races in one: the 'Garnet' Cup for novices is also part of the programme. In the event, an under strength Belgrave team missed out on London medals for the first time in living memory, despite a back to some-kind-of-form effort from Carl Lawton, who made light work of the twists and turns of the traffic free course, and a sterling effort in the women's 5k from Sue Porter who secured a London Champs. bronze. Men's 10m 1, M.Easton (Surrey WC) 70:52; 2, S.Phillips (Ilford) 74:28; 3, C.Cheeseman (Surrey WC) 75:58; ... 9, C.Lawton 83:23; 19, P.Warburton 89:47; 29, D.Fotheringham 95:46; 37, J.Dunsford 98:59. Teams: 1, Surrey WC 11; 2, Ilford 23; 3, Trowbridge 42; ... 5, Belgrave 57 (4th in London Champs.). Women's 5k 1, S.Brown (Surrey) 26:13; 2, N.Parsons (Aldershot F&D) 29:23; 3, K.Wallace (Cambridge H) 29:45; ... 7, S.Porter 30:29 (3rd in Southern and London) SUSSEX, SURREY & KENT 10m CHAMPS., STEYNING, 27 FEB Down in deepest Sussex over a tough 3k circuit Carl Lawton became our first county 10 mile champion of the weekend. 1, N.Carmody (Cambridge H) 76:24; 2, C.Lawton (Belgrave/ 1st Sry) 80:54; 3, P.Hannell (Surrey WC) 81:29. Reports by Carl Lawton and Paul Warburton MIDDLESEX, BUCKS & HERTS 10m CHAMPS., ENFIELD 28 FEB Four in a row for John Hall who may hold some kind of enviable record for being the closest competing athlete in Great Britain to the start line of an official race. Can anyone do better than 160 metres from front door to start line? On a bitter, sleet ridden day, our man from the ministry was well served by his thermal tights, eventually leading both Middlesex and Belgrave to an easy win. 1, J.Hall (Belgrave) 80:43; 2, D.Cross, (Verlea) 82:17; 3, S.Lightman (Surrey WC) 85:15; ... 6, D.Fotheringham 92:18; 11, J.Dunsford 98:30. Middlesex teams: 1, Belgrave. NATIONAL 20k CHAMPS./ WORLD CUP TRIALS, CARDIFF, 14 MAR Held on an exciting 20 lap circuit of 500metres up and 500 metres back on the same stretch of road, this must pose the question of where British walking is going. Only 50 or so finished; it was supposed to be a trial but did not really come up with a satisfactory result. The one positive outcome was that only four of the first twenty were vets. and the course was at least in pleasant surroundings and completely traffic free. This National is usually held in May and on a Saturday so one must ask if the walkers did not turn out because of these changes. Belgrave began the year on the right foot by starting a team and finishing one, just. 1, A.Penn (Coventry) 1:25:57; 2, D.Stone (Steyning) 1:26:59; 3, M.Rush (Lakeland) 1:28:54; ... 20, C.Lawton 1:45:07; 40, D.Fotheringham 2:00:48; 45, P.Duncan 2:05:41; 50, J.Dunsford 2:11:43. Teams: 6, Belgrave. SOUTHERN AREA 20k CHAMPS., WIMBLEDON, 3 APR The Bels picked up the silver medals behind Surrey Walking Club but the race was very disappointing in that the lowest ever number of finishers in this event, ten, made it to the finish line. Of these, two were guests. 1, N.Carmody (Cambridge H) 1:37:16; 2, C.Bradley (Trowbridge gst) 1:42:23; 3, A.Seddon (Enfield gst) 1:44:39; ... 5, C.Lawton (3rd in Champs) 1:51:56; 8, D.Fotheringham 1:58:42; 10, J.Dunsford 2:07:22. Teams: 1, Surrey WC 11; 2, Belgrave 16. Above top: The start of the Belgrave Open '7', nearly won this year by Julie Drake. Another year and another race - how many times has Carl climbed Cottenham Park Road in his Racewalking career? Bottom left to right: Easily the best looking of the walking crew (well, the photographer thinks so anyway) - Paul Warburton. The Man from the Ministry and race winner (just) John Hall. Pat Duncan - "What sort of a person is it anyway, who'd park themselves right at the steepest part of the blinkin' hill to take their pictures. Let's hope old 'Kingy' will be racing up this hill again soon, fully recovered from his motorbike accident. items.sum: Three club notes: Ray Hall added as walking coach, Gordon Doubleday home after a diabetes diagnosis, and a Belgrave advert in CBI News seeking sponsors.
items.s: Three club notes: Ray Hall added as walking coach, Gordon Doubleday home after a diabetes diagnosis, and a Belgrave advert in CBI News seeking sponsors. You will notice that for the first time in many a year we have listed our Club Coaches on the summer fixture card. And of course, what is the obvious thing that happens? - we leave someone out. Sorry Ray! Let us make amends by declaring that Ray Hall, coaching walking, will be in attendance at Battersea Park. We understand that Gordon Doubleday has spent a little time in hospital where he has been found to be diabetic. However, he is now back home and we hope that his complaint is not troubling him too much. There, in the March issue of CBI News, sharing a page with an article on "World Development Awards" and another describing how British managers should be equipped to do business in Japan, was a startlingly different advert. "Belgrave Harriers - UK champions" it was headed, and showed the well-known Mark Shearman colour photograph of John Regis passing the baton to Jon Ridgeon that graced the cover of our own magazine a few issues back. The advertisement was the idea of Bill Laws, hoping to find a UK firm for whom we could do promotional work while in Hungary for the European Clubs Cup Final, and of course also aiming at potential sponsors. Let's hope that the calculating mind of some captain of industry is grabbed by the idea, for we are currently one of the very few top clubs without a sponsor of any kind. items.label: April 1993
items.sum: Alan Mead's eyewitness recollection, as a 16-year-old fan, of Stan Vickers breaking George Larner's 1904 UK 2 miles walk record with 13:02.4 against Ken Matthews at the 1960 AAA Championships at the White City, with notes on the 1960 Rome and 1964 Tokyo Olympic walks.
items.s: The Record Breaker Alan Mead's eyewitness recollection, as a 16-year-old fan, of Stan Vickers breaking George Larner's 1904 UK 2 miles walk record with 13:02.4 against Ken Matthews at the 1960 AAA Championships at the White City, with notes on the 1960 Rome and 1964 Tokyo Olympic walks. The Record Breaker I had set out hours ago, having walked to the bus-stop at the Malden Roundabout and then ridden the number 72 route all the way to Shepherd's Bush, dispatching a "hay stack" of corned beef and tomato sandwiches long before crossing the river at Hammersmith. There was a great confluence of athletics fans in Wood Lane. Thousands, like me, were trekking up from the "Bush", and hordes poured out of the tube station. All had come to the White City to be at the 1960 AAA Championships and watch the likes of Peter Radford, Milkha Singh and Gordon Pirie go through their paces in preparation for the forthcoming Rome Olympics. Belgrave had some pretty good sprinters and middle-distance men in those far off days and I was keen to see them in action but in 1960 the Belgrave Walking Section was supreme. Walking Secretary Jack Goswell was able to deploy some half a dozen internationals in team races and they had swept all before them - the Leicester '20', RWA '20', RWA '50' - all had featured 'BELGRAVE H' at the top of the result sheet. This day was going to give me the chance to see one of those heroes, Stan Vickers, in combat with his Midland rival Ken Matthews of Royal Sutton Coldfield. Both were to duel in the walker's sprint - the 2 miles. Both were in superb form and the likelihood was that the UK record of 13:11.4, set 56 years earlier on 13th July 1904 by George E. Larner, was going to go. High up on the concrete terracing of that draughty stadium, now long gone, I had a bird's-eye view of the arena. The dull red clay track contrasted with the surrounding grass oval of the greyhound-racing circuit that separated the fans from the competitors. No digital results display-screen in 1960 of course, but a huge white results board and a large clock with a sweep second hand by which one could judge the athletes' progress versus the record book. The three weeks before the event had already seen some astounding 2 mile walk times. At Motspur Park in the Southern Champs. Stan had won in his best ever time of 13:31.8, beating his own championship best by 17 seconds. On the same day Matthews had taken the Midland title, also in a championship best, with 13:36. Just a few days later in a club match against the Stock Exchange at Battersea the Belgravian had gone faster still with 13:26.4 and then, the very next Saturday, on Peterborough's grass track, Ken and Stan clashed in an invitation race where the latter confidently sprinted to victory and actually equalled Larner's 1904 record. Again at Battersea, on the Wednesday night preceding the AAA, the record withstood another assault as Vickers scorched to a time just one fifth of a second slower. Surely that time would crumble today. Eighteen men faced the starter and the four East Germans, Lindner, Hildebrand, Adolph and Pathus, together with the Sikhs Zora and Adjit Singh, made it a truly international field. Stan was not the only Belgravian in the line-up as Eric Hall was also hoping to impress. The start was unbelievably fast. At the gun Zora Singh tore into the lead and after a single circuit the timekeepers logged lap one at 1:34.3 - that's 12:34 pace! Matthews and Vickers were in tow and then came Colin Williams, Adjit Singh and Lindner. But the inevitable happened, Zora had thrown caution to the winds with his effort and after half a mile the judges pulled him out, a fate that soon befell his fellow countryman and two of the Germans. Now it was the powerful Matthews blasting along at the front with Vickers so close behind him that they were later described as "siamese twins". The mile came up - 6:30.2 - had such a time ever been recorded before? Williams was now in trouble some 15 seconds behind and was soon to be swept up by Lindner and Hall. It was obvious that the burly Sutton Coldfield man was out to avenge that defeat of the previous week but how on earth could he keep such a pace going. One of these two must crack soon. Further laps of 99 to 100 seconds unreeled - one and a half miles in 9:51.4. I can't remember a walk before or since causing such an uproar from the crowd. Still only one yard covered the two protagonists as the strident clangour of the last lap bell cut through the cheers. Ken Matthews needed just one more lap in 1:40.5 to take the record but something in the angular frame of the man in his wake foretold of more drama to come. Stan suddenly veered out and round the Midlander in an all-out heel and toe sprint. For an instant Matthews seemed stunned before he too released every remaining spark of energy left in his body. Vickers had taken twenty yards by the back straight and as the final turn was approached, spectators were torn between the vision of Ken Matthews desperately trying to get back into contention, Stan Vickers racing towards the finish line, and that giant second-hand on the result board, sweeping inexorably on towards the top of the clock and the 13 minute mark. Tumultuous cheers reached an even greater volume as the Belgrave Harrier crossed the line. He had clearly smashed the record and for an instant it seemed that he might have even gone under 13 minutes. Within a short while it was announced that Larner's time had been beaten by 9 seconds and that Matthews too had gone inside the old mark. 1, S.E.Vickers (Belgrave) 13:02.4 (UK and AAA National Record); 2, K.J.Matthews (Royal Sutton Coldfield) 13:09.6; 3, D.Lindner (E.Germany); 4, E.W.Hall (Belgrave) 13:51.8. It's a sobering thought that Stan's time was worth around 12:09 for the modern-day equivalent of the race - 3,000 metres. That day at the White City was, of course, just a landmark on the road to greater glory for several of the competitors. In the sweltering heat of the Rome Olympics where just about every British distance athlete performed well below par, Stan became the 20 kilometre Walk bronze medallist in 1 hour 34 minutes and 57 seconds, 49 seconds behind the great Soviet Champion Golubnichiy. At the half-way point Stan had passed a badly suffering Ken Matthews who commanded a 19 second lead at one stage, only to falter in the conditions and later require hospital treatment. Eric Hall also posted an excellent performance in that Rome race, coming home 10th. Ken's day of Olympic triumph came four years later at the Tokyo Games when it was his turn to win gold with Lindner 2nd. But back on that July Saturday evening in 1960 it just remained for a 16 year old Belgravian to walk back to Shepherd's Bush and wait for the bus, head a-buzzing with the excitement of seeing a fellow Club member setting a UK record. items.label: April 1993
items.sum: Terry Lawton's light-hearted account of seven Belgrave runners' Easter racing trip to Guernsey: a six mile road race, five miles cross country, a two mile cross country relay and a half-marathon in which Helen Maskrey won the ladies' prize and overall title.
items.s: Seven go to Guernsey Terry Lawton's light-hearted account of seven Belgrave runners' Easter racing trip to Guernsey: a six mile road race, five miles cross country, a two mile cross country relay and a half-marathon in which Helen Maskrey won the ladies' prize and overall title. Seven go to Guernsey How did you spend Easter this year? Seven of us went to Guernsey for four days of racing. We met at Gatwick, except for 'Wassie', who must have known something was up because we had a four hour delay (he went from Heathrow). Don also must have known something, having booked for a later flight but arriving two hours before us. "Just smell that sea air," said Fred, to which Michelin-man Ross replied, "Stuff the sea air - where's our hotel?" Helen went for a drive and promptly got lost due to a lack of signposts and it wasn't long before the rest of us were in similar trouble. We only had to travel three miles to book in for our races but returned after an hour having driven nineteen miles and still not found the place to register. Why no signposts? Something to do with confusing the enemy in the last war! Six mile road race. Good Friday dawned, grey, misty and miserable. We left for the race armed with excuses in true Belgravian tradition. Fred reminded us that he was getting over an injury, "so I'll be coach". 'Michelin' was complaining about his achilles problems while Carl, who hadn't actually run for a year, decided to stay behind and do some shopping. Wiser than yesterday we elected 'Squaddie' Don as navigator, "Cos he's a trained soldier and leader of men," said 'Coach'. It was a good choice and we arrived on time. The course was billed as undulating but could have been considered mountainous. "What time are you expecting to run it in, 'Squaddie'?" I asked. "Oh! about 38 minutes. Do you want to follow me?" "Great, thanks," I said, and then he promptly blasted home in 36 minutes, forcing 'Michelin' and I to run 12:30 for the first two miles. We later seized on this as one of our excuses for 'blowing up'. Results: Don 36:10, Helen 36:40 (4th lady), 'Wassie' 38:12, Terry 42:24, Ross 44:55. Five miles cross country Saturday arrived wet and windy. Carl decided that today he would look after the kit and 'Coach', who had seen a lady in blue shorts, suddenly forgot all about his injury and in chasing her had the most enjoyable run of the day! "Hey! Carl. How did my dry kit get wet?" "I don't know. It must have been wet when you gave it to me." 'Coach', always one to drop someone else in it, revealed the truth: "He was sitting on it". Results: Don 29:32, Helen 30:24 (pb for this course and 3rd lady overall), 'Wassie' 31:34, Terry 32:34, Ross 35:10. Two mile cross country relay The course for Sunday's race was muddy, hilly and very wet. Carl stayed in the hotel to rest from the exertion of carrying my wet kit! Don ran his heart out and had to sit down afterwards to recuperate. It was the first time he had rested all week. Helen ran hard, looked cool and actually enjoyed it. She taunted me as I approached the finish: "Where's that famous sprint now?" So I kicked and got a pb. Thanks 'Mummy Bunny'. 'Michelin' left his shoes in the mud and finished in his socks - well actually they were mine. 'Wassie' ran for the 'Stragglers' but the Bels team beat them. 'Coach' advised us that the team would probably be at their peak in September but I thought I ran well and wasn't the only one - "Even 'Wassie' with his sun-lamp and bull-worker couldn't beat rising star Terry," said 'Squaddie'. 'Wassie' was seen throwing muddy old socks into the hedge but they were later rescued by 'Squaddie' to take home for Keith Duckett, although Helen quipped that they would't be old enough for him. Results: Don 12:31, Helen 12:56 (pb and fastest lady), Terry 14:00, 'Wassie' 14:02, Ross 15:28. Half-Marathon Our worst fears were met as we gathered for the start of the half-marathon. The wind was so strong that all thoughts of pbs. evaporated. 'Michelin' bravely offered to run in place of our gallant 'Squaddie' who lay sick in bed with beads of perspiration on his forehead, having given all for the Bels. the day before. For Helen there was a dilemma. She was joint leader overall, so should she now lead from the start or sit behind her rivals and then pounce at the end. Urged on by 'Coach' she determinedly led from the gun. After a few miles she was caught by a local male runner who patronisingly said, "stay with me luv and I'll get you round". Well, it was like a red rag to a bull. Our Helen dropped the foolish man when he hesitated at the first waterhole. "Eat dirt, sucker," she muttered. At the half-way turn-around she passed me with a cheery call, her rivals now 200 metres behind. Storming home she took the first ladies prize, won the ladies' overall title and even had the energy to join 'Squaddie', who had now risen from his sick-bed, to cheer the rest of us over the line. Results: Helen 1:24, 'Wassie' 1:27:25, Terry 1:39:10, Ross 1:52:03 ('Boofer' please note). A great time. Why not join us next year? Terry Lawton The seven were John Wasbrough, Terry Lawton, Helen Maskrey, Don Anderson, Carl Cross, Fred Paget and Ross Martin. items.sum: Archive photo of the finish of the half-mile handicap at a Belgrave Harriers meeting at Battersea Park in May 1929, won by Tom Pritchard, with Charlie Jones's recollections.
items.s: May 1929 Archive photo of the finish of the half-mile handicap at a Belgrave Harriers meeting at Battersea Park in May 1929, won by Tom Pritchard, with Charlie Jones's recollections. May 1929 It's May 1929 and the crowds have again turned out in force to watch an athletic meeting put on at Battersea Park Athletic Track by the Belgrave Harriers. The half-mile handicap was a close affair up front with Tom Pritchard just triumphing over Alf Club of Kent A.C., and T.C. "Charlie" Jones in 3rd place. All three were well clear of Ernie Duffett and Joe Coleman who can be seen in the distance and the winning time was 1 minute 59 and 4-5th seconds. The photograph appeared on the back page of a subsequent "Daily Mirror" and Charlie Jones has kept his copy of the picture safe these 64 years since. Charlie recalls that the first meeting he ever saw was in 1921, also at Battersea, when Micky Pyer won a mile championship race. In those days there was a putting green where the car park now is, and for big meetings the Club used to get permission to erect a marquee on it for changing facilities. Now that we have re-published the photo' it will go into Belgrave's growing archive of such items, currently looked after by Clive Shippen. items.sum: Letter to Derek Crookes from Stan Scarsbrook, an 84-year-old former Surrey AC runner living in Scotland, recalling his career and Belgrave contemporaries, printed under the letters heading "Write on!".
items.s: Enjoyed all of it Letter to Derek Crookes from Stan Scarsbrook, an 84-year-old former Surrey AC runner living in Scotland, recalling his career and Belgrave contemporaries, printed under the letters heading "Write on!". Write on! Enjoyed all of it The following was received by Derek Crookes as a result of an enquiry from an old worthy of Surrey AC who wondered what had happened to his Club. As a Life Member of Surrey, his name has been added to our mailing list. Dear Mr. Crookes, Thank you for giving my grandson the information regarding Surrey AC. I have been in Scotland for 19 years. I still follow athletics and I wondered what had happened. I am 84 and still take an active part in sport, playing golf now and again. I have won the Senior Championship twice and even had a "hole in one". I always think of the good times I had when running and enjoyed all of it - the friendships with other athletes and the good competitions we had. I knew A. Penny, B. Footer and C. Carter of Belgrave well. I had a lucky career - Sussex 3 miles champion, Empire Games steeplechase and lots of other races. I was an Army runner also. I remember Mr. Vowles very well. Surrey AC made me a Life Member in 1935. I wish your club all the very best and hope you win more trophies. My best regards to A. Penny and any of the old Belgrave Lads. Stan Scarsbrook, Peeblesshire. items.h: ... But we are taken to task
items.sum: Letter from Doris M. Dean taking ARM to task over the November 1992 article on E.F. Vowles of Surrey Athletic Club, saying Vowles would have been horrified at the 1982 amalgamation with Belgrave.
items.s: ... But we are taken to task Letter from Doris M. Dean taking ARM to task over the November 1992 article on E.F. Vowles of Surrey Athletic Club, saying Vowles would have been horrified at the 1982 amalgamation with Belgrave. ... But we are taken to task Dear Editors, It was a pleasure to receive the November '92 issue of "The Belgravian" and congratulations on a very informative and interesting magazine. As you can imagine, being an old stalwart of Surrey Athletic Club, I was most interested in your article regarding Mr. E.F. Vowles - 'The Grand Old Man of Athletics', but I would take ARM to task when he states at the end of the article that "were Mr. Vowles alive today he would be proud of the contribution his clubmen have made in forming part of a team ... etc., etc." 'V' would have been horrified to think his members would ever contemplate being anything other than Surrey AC. He breathed and lived Surrey Athletic Club, it was his baby, his family and his life - sometimes to the exclusion of his own family. He died in impoverished circumstances in his 95th year, having given his money and health to athletics over many years and I for one am more than pleased that he was not alive in August 1982 when members of that era decided to amalgamate with the Belgrave Harriers. I knew Mr. Vowles very well and visited him up to the time of his death and am still in touch with his family, so I think I can safely say I knew how he felt about Surrey Athletic Club and I am sorry that ARM did not finish his excellent article after "his eightieth year". items.sum: Letter from Gordon Doubleday recalling his wartime years: evacuation to Exeter, running for Exeter H., the 1942 Poly Marathon, Syd Ring's London-Brighton relay mishap, and Harry Parker producing The Belgravian in wartime.
items.s: 'Doub' recalls '42 Letter from Gordon Doubleday recalling his wartime years: evacuation to Exeter, running for Exeter H., the 1942 Poly Marathon, Syd Ring's London-Brighton relay mishap, and Harry Parker producing The Belgravian in wartime. 'Doub' recalls '42 Dear Editors, As usual I enjoyed my visit to Wimbledon for the Club's Open Walk. Carl gave me "Something to read on the train," which, of course, was "The Belgravian". Under the title "50 Years Ago" I see my return to London mentioned. For those not around those 50 years ago perhaps I'd better explain. When WW2 broke out (Sep'39) my firm evacuated my wife, baby daughter and myself to Exeter where we had an emergency lab. in case our London premises (Bishopsgate) got "bombed" - which they did. When Exeter was "bombed" (April '42) we were moved back to London. I joined Exeter H. There was little competition but we were allowed as guest runners in events held by University College of the S.W. and St. Lukes Teacher Training College. Both of these are now part of Exeter University. I used to try and manage a Saturday run and a midweek one. The day I came back to London was the 1,000th day of the war - also in time to enter the Poly Marathon. I had gained standard medals (3 1/2 hrs) in the '38 and '39 events from Windsor to the Poly track at Chiswick. The war time Polys were held on the four lap course from Chiswick. In 1942 they decided to award medals on the basis of one for every six entrants (there were 90). I had the joy of picking off a few stragglers on the last lap to finish 15th - the last of the medal winners! As mentioned club mate Syd Ring was second. Syd was very meticulous regarding his running. He once did the stage on the London-Brighton Relay which included the level crossing at Crawley. He looked up time tables and worked out that if things went as planned the gates would be open when he was due. Unfortunately, as he approached the gates they closed for an unscheduled goods train, so he had to use the pedestrian subway. He took it all very calmly. Back to myself! When the war began I had settled down as Hon. Editor of "The Belgravian", but, being away from London, was unable to continue. Luckily our Asst Hon. Secretary Harry Parker not only produced wartime Belgravians, but summer and winter fixture lists. These were condensed onto postcards - in any case newsprint was hard to come by, but Harry managed it. After the war Harry became President of the E.C.C.U. but, sadly, died during his term of office. On my return to London I was able to help Harry with "The Belgravian". We tried to get the mag. to all members, especially those on active service abroad. Alf would have been delighted Dear Editors, Thank you very much indeed for sending me a copy of "The Belgravian". It was interesting to see what it had grown into - most impressive. Alf would have been delighted with it. I have kept in touch with some of his contemporaries, though sadly, numbers are dwindling. Win Martin Shepherd writes every Christmas to tell me the year's news and I appreciate her letters. It's good to know that the Club continues to do well. With all best wishes for many further successes. Nancy Harley, Uxbridge Nancy Harley Nancy Harley Alf Alf Win Martin Shepherd Win Martin Shepherd Uxbridge

items.sum: Poem "One-Track Mind" by Ernest Obeng, from his Runner's Primer of Poetry, in which a partner complains about a runner's obsession.
items.s: One track mind Poem "One-Track Mind" by Ernest Obeng, from his Runner's Primer of Poetry, in which a partner complains about a runner's obsession. One track mind - a Runner's Primer of Poetry by Ernest Obeng One-Track Mind "You've got a one-track mind," she said. "You're always on the run. Why don't you stop and use your head. There are other kinds of fun. I don't know why you have to wake the household up at dawn to jog for miles to sweat and ache, and come home looking drawn. Why don't you use your energy on something else for once. Just face up to reality and give the world a chance. When you get injured or don't win, you take it out on us, pretend you hold your feelings in but love to have us fuss. What pleasant evenings we spend; you're either fast asleep Or trying out the latest trend That's hit the athlete's heap. I'd love to sit and talk instead, but then you have the knack of using anything I've said to talk some more of track. You've got a one-track mind," she moaned. Before she'd said some more, I'd put my shoes on, tied my lace, and jogged out through the door. Published with the Ernie's kind permission Ernest Obeng Ernest Obeng Ernest Obeng Ernie

items.s: 1948 Arthur Bruce's recollection of the 1948 athletics year: Wooderson's National cross country win over Vic Blowfield with Belgrave taking the team title, the London to Brighton Relay, the AAA Championships, the London Olympic Games day by day, and Belgrave's Olympians (Harry Churcher, Bill Nankeville, Bill Lucas, Etienne Gailly) and season, illustrated with a 1948 Elliman Athletic Rub advert, the Olympic programme cover and emblem, and an Ed. Lacey photo of Len Herbert and Bill Lucas. 1948 by Arthur Bruce 1948! A year that conjures up pictures of titanic struggles climaxing in the first Post War Olympic Games in austerity ridden Britain with eager athletes deprived of Olympic competition since 1936, anxious to prove themselves. Arthur Bruce continues his tales of athletics from the post-war years. After two post war seasons a pattern of World Athletics had solidified. And when the Games were ushered in on Friday 30th July 1948 at the newly laid track at Wembley Stadium, armed with our daily shilling (5p) programme, we were geared for a feast of athletics. Wooderson's "National" The British winter season that had preceded the Olympics had produced a number of post war stars to which had been added Sydney Wooderson, who after a magnificent track season of 1946 had professed his intention to finish his career by attempting to win the National Cross Country title. Starting with an exploratory season in 1947, he entered 1948 with his running programme geared to the National in March at Graves Park, Sheffield. He achieved his objective after a tremendous struggle with our own Vic Blowfield, only taking the lead in the finishing funnel. Belgrave won the team race with 154 points beating their conquerors of 1947, Sutton Harriers by 20 points. The Bels scoring six were home in 57 places. Wooderson's subsequent performance in the International at Reading was disappointing, and coupled with the English team being comfortably beaten by the Belgians who were led by surprise winner, Jean Doms. For Wooderson it was the end of a brilliant career dating back to his public school mile win in the early 'thirties. The year progressed to a short road relay season climaxing in April with the classic London to Brighton Relay which produced another great club struggle, with Bill Lucas taking Belgrave into the lead over Birchfield on the last stage into Brighton. The track season The track season was of course organised along simpler lines than today, with only the British Games and Inter-Counties at Whitsun weekend to interrupt the progression of County and District leading to the AAA Championships and selection for the Olympic Games held in the first week of July. The principal talking points in early season were the hopes of McDonald Bailey, the Trinidadian born sprinter who had elected to run for Britain and who had shown such good form since 1946. This year, however, he was plagued with injuries and confronted by a new star. Alastair McCorquadale arrived suddenly on the sprinting scene, beating Bailey in the Kinnaird Trophy meeting. The other major talking point concerned Roger Bannister, the new Oxford discovery, who had been a surprise inter-varsity mile winner in 1947. Bannister wisely had turned down any thought of running in the 1948 Games, preferring to work to a long term plan for 1952 and Helsinki. The AAA Championships proved to be as exciting as predicted. The 100yds provided a win for John Treloar the Australian sprint hope who just edged out McCorquadale and Bailey. McCorquadale returned to win the 220yds. Another Australian prodigy, Morris Curotta, won the 440yds from the best Britain could offer. The 880yds, probably the finest race of the Championships, seemed to be a struggle between Arthur Wint and the visiting New Zealand Champion Doug Harris until a few yards from the tape when both were overwhelmed by John Parlett's late surge. Bill Nankeville (Belgrave) gained the first of his four 1 mile titles with Roger Bannister in his Championship debut, in 5th place. Other titles to go abroad were the 3 miles won by Wooderson's old rival Willie Slykhuis, the Dutch star, and the High and Long jumps to visiting Australian Olympians. The most promising performance from Britain's point of view was the win by the 18 year old schoolboy J.Burrell in the 120yds hurdles, beating several established stars. One could say that the British Olympic team possessed a number of possible winners while the opposition was difficult to gauge. The "Games" The Olympic Games were four weeks later, with 53 Nations providing 815 athletes. They were without Germany, Japan, Russia and most of the African Continent - a compact affair but of high quality nevertheless. The opening day revealed the strength of the American team, especially in the sprints, 800 metres and 400 metre hurdles, with Britain's sprinters and middle distance runners also qualifying. The climax of the day was the revelation of the Games, Lt. Emil Zatopek of the Czech Army who demolished the field in the 10,000 metres, winning by over three-quarters of a minute and breaking the legend of the Finnish runners in this event, a distance they had dominated for over twenty years. Day two, Saturday July 31st, threw up a surprise winner in the 100 metres. Gold medallist was the American third string Harrison Dillard, in reality a World class hurdler. Our two hopefuls McCorquadale and McDonald Bailey made the final and were 5th and 6th respectively. John Parlett excelled himself with a time of 1:50 to qualify for the 800m final while the US produced yet another world class hurdler in Ray Cochran to take the 400m hurdle title in 51.1, a new record. Monday brought Fanny Blankers-Koen the first of her four wins as she took the 100m for Holland. Mal Whitfield retained the US grip on the 800m by holding off Arthur Wint in a close finish and the day ended with Emil Zatopek just failing to catch Gaston Reiff of Belgium in monsoon-like conditions in the 5,000m, after appearing well beaten. On Wednesday the stream of excellent performances continued with Blankers-Koen beating our own Maureen Gardner narrowly in the 80m hurdles for her second gold medal. Finland had their expected win in the men's Javelin and the USA made a clean sweep in the 110m hurdles, Bill Porter winning in 13.9. The strength of Swedish steeplechasing was shown on the Thursday, with the first three home led by Sjoestrand in 9.04. This was followed by a memorable 400m final in which Herb McKenley was overtaken in the straight by his fellow Jamaican Arthur Wint, the 800m silver medallist. Friday, and after another downpour yet another favourite, the World 1,500m record holder Lennart Strand was held off by his fellow Swede Henry Eriksson; our own Bill Nankeville finished a meritorious 6th in 3.52. The other final that day saw Blankers-Koen win her third gold in the 200m from Britain's Audrey Williamson. The last day provided the expected relay wins in the men's events by the United States, the longer relay somewhat luckily after Arthur Wint pulled a muscle on the third stage while making inroads into the American lead. The women's sprint relay went to Holland, giving Fanny Blankers-Koen gold medal number four, and the Decathlon showed the world the new American discovery Bob Mathias, who at the tender age of 17 upstaged his more experienced rivals. Both walks went to Sweden but only after much dispute amongst the judges which cast a cloud over future track walks. The grand finale, the Marathon, provided its usual high drama with Cabrera of Argentina catching Belgium's Etienne Gailly four hundred metres from the tape closely, followed by Britain's Tommy Richards, who had run a very sensible race. Belgrave Olympians Belgrave's involvement in these stirring events were a fine 5th place in the 10,000m track walk by Harry Churcher, Bill Nankeville's equally good 6th place in the 1,500m final and Bill Lucas' run in the 5,000m heats where he was unfortunate to draw Zatopek's heat. A word should also be said about the marathon runner Etienne Gailly, for while in England in the Army, he had run for Belgrave. The runners were not Belgrave's only contribution, as a scrutiny of the programmes exhibited a number of Belgrave officials among the judges, announcers and officials who had made the Games such a success. Team performances by the Bels during the year were first rate. Major titles over the Country included the Surrey, Southern and National titles, coupled with the South of Thames Senior and the principal road relay of the year, the London to Brighton. The walkers maintained their usual high standard by winning the National 10 mile Championship and also took the Surrey title. In the remainder of the walking Championships they were only thwarted by the excellent Sheffield and Surrey teams. On the track, excluding those already mentioned in the Games, a number of excellent performances were produced. Alan Sexton ran a classic race to win the AAA Junior 220yd title and evergreen Charlie Smart, home on leave from Germany, finished 5th in the AAA 6 mile Championships, only a few yards away from Olympic selection. On studying the results of the closed Belgrave events and Championships one is stuck by the depth in all sections of the club and the support given to club handicaps and Championships, and the keen competition for places in Belgrave teams. Arthur Bruce Len Herbert and Bill Lucas were often involved in battle royal. Len, who gained his international vest in 1946, invariably used to sit in on the taller, longer striding Bill, waiting to turn on his powerful sprint in the final stretch. But on this occasion, believed to be at Wimbledon Stadium in 1951, Bill held the sprinter at bay. W.E. "Bill "Lucas, DFC, made his international debut in the heats of the 1948 Olympic 5,000m. KENT AND SURREY CHAMPS., CRYSTAL PALACE, 19 SEP Owain Lewes reports:- This year Blackheath Harriers revived their traditional relays, moved them to September and combined the Kent and Surrey Championships on their interesting and testing course at Crystal Palace. The result was a far more entertaining and competitive event than the Surrey relays of recent years. Belgrave finished 14th in the six stage Senior event out of an entry of 40 teams, however they were 5th amongst the Surrey based clubs. Gary Staines ran the first leg for Belgrave, making his first appearance since his injury in December 1991, clocking the second fastest leg of the day behind Blackheath's in form Gary Arthey.
