items.s: THE YACHT HANDICAP, WIMBLEDON, 3 OCT ARM's account of the 1992 'Yacht' Handicap at Wimbledon, won by 17-year-old Stuart Booth, with new Belgravian Kaessa Tadesse running 14:36 from an 11:15 handicap for third on the all-time list, and the full handicap result. THE YACHT HANDICAP, WIMBLEDON, 3 OCT A steady drizzle did little to dampen the spirits of young Stuart Booth who must have thought it was his birthday when he found the handicapper ushering him towards the front of the indian file making up the start of the 1992 'Yacht' Handicap. But this was not the only talking point among the bystanders: a new Belgravian, Junior World Half-marathon Champion Kaessa Tadesse, an Ethiopian now settling in the UK, was making his Belgrave debut, and the field contained four ladies out to settle a few scores with male colleagues. By the time the front marker was away the field was up to 21, disappointingly four down on the previous race. Pat Mead set off as "rabbit", a little cast down to find that Charlie Manning was a non-starter after she had voiced a pointed, "I'll see you in the 'Yacht 3'," after a recent training clash. Dennis Jones was next away and then came a short wait until a gaggle around the six-minute mark were sent off, Stuart among them and grinning like the Cheshire Cat as he rounded the turn at the end of Lauriston Road. On they came: the veterans, the faster ladies, the younger men, until Marco and Marcello brought up what would normally have been the back of the field, penalised by well over 10 minutes. As "March" disappeared along South Side and headed for the Memorial we waited ... and waited ... until at last Kaessa, suffering from an 11 minute 15 second handicap, came by looking every inch a champion. "Surely no-one can give away that much in a three mile race," says your reporter. "Don't you believe it old son," replies Mr. Carter, "but watch out, he don't know the way!" as Kaessa attempted to turn left and head for Raynes Park. The wait. Rain dripping from trees crept under collars and into shoes and the recorder's ball-point pen gave up the ghost as speculation continued: "Wonder if Stuart's got time to stop and take a rest ... Hope Kaessa sees Marcello turn onto Windmill Road - otherwise he'll end up in Putney." "They're at the village," went up the cry, and yes, it was Stuart Booth, well clear to take the race by no less than 1 minute and 9 seconds. But while Handicapper "Boofer" Bruce may have slipped up with the winner, his assessment of the majority of the field proved to be first rate as the front markers, although still to the fore along West Side, were being eaten up by the pack. Jim Slough and Chris Taplin were fairly comfortably 2nd and 3rd Belgravians but then came a frenzy of activity with a dozen or more all on the finishing path at the same time and Kaessa striking through the lot of them like a knife. What a run! His 14:36 took him straight up to third spot on the all-time top 20 list behind Gerry North's epic 14:15 in 1962 and Ollie Foote's 14:34 from 1984 - and he's just 17 years old! items.h: REEBOK SURREY LEAGUE DIV. 1 RACE 1, BROCKWELL PARK, 10 OCT
items.sum: A weakened Belgrave team finished 8th in the first Surrey League Division 1 race at Brockwell Park, won by guest runner Joseph Njugana, with Jim Estall first Belgravian in 23rd.
items.s: REEBOK SURREY LEAGUE DIV. 1 RACE 1, BROCKWELL PARK, 10 OCT A weakened Belgrave team finished 8th in the first Surrey League Division 1 race at Brockwell Park, won by guest runner Joseph Njugana, with Jim Estall first Belgravian in 23rd. REEBOK SURREY LEAGUE DIV. 1 RACE 1, BROCKWELL PARK, 10 OCT With many of last year's regular team members missing through injury, work, or study commitments, Belgrave turned up with rather a weak team and could only finish 8th, our lowest placing in the Surrey league since we were relegated from division one four years ago. The press made much of the participation of two guest runners; Joseph Njugana, a Kenyan brought to the race by John Bicourt, ran without a number and won with ease and Dave Taylor, a Blackheath athlete, came an unofficial 4th. Three laps of the undulating Brockwell Park course is a good test of Autumn fitness especially after the heavy rain we have had this season, and in spite of the lowly team performance there were some encouraging Belgrave performances. Jim Estall ran his usual steady, reliable race and James Ryle, in his first Cross Country season for the club, did well to finish in the top fifty after perhaps a rather ambitious start. Roger Alsop, fresh from a very good track season, ran intelligently, starting cautiously and moving through the field to 55th using his speed on the downhill sections to good effect. items.sum: Paul Evans finished 11th in 61:38 in the Great North Run, which incorporated the first IAAF World Half Marathon Championships, and Kaessa Tadesse, soon to join Belgrave, won the IAAF Junior Half Marathon the day before.
items.s: GREAT NORTH RUN, NEWCASTLE TO SOUTH SHIELDS, 20 SEP Paul Evans finished 11th in 61:38 in the Great North Run, which incorporated the first IAAF World Half Marathon Championships, and Kaessa Tadesse, soon to join Belgrave, won the IAAF Junior Half Marathon the day before. GREAT NORTH RUN, NEWCASTLE TO SOUTH SHIELDS, 20 SEP This year's Great North run incorporated the inaugural IAAF World Half Marathon Championships. Belgrave's Olympic 10,000m representative Paul Evans, ran another splendid race to finish 11th in 61:38 - second Briton home behind Rossendale's Dave Lewis, 7th. The race was won by Kenya's Benson Masya in an astounding 60:24 and only 16 men from the UK featured in the first 100. Paul's time was only four seconds outside his pb set in Lisbon over a course thought to be 50 metres short so he felt pretty pleased with his effort. The previous day Kaessa Tadesse, soon to join Belgrave, won the IAAF Junior Half Marathon Championship in the very impressive time of 64.51. items.sum: Mark Anderson's report of the South of Thames Junior cross country championships at Margate, where Belgrave were 3rd in the 4-man team event with Jim Estall 8th and James Ryle 10th.
items.s: SOUTH OF THAMES JUN. CC CHAMPS., MARGATE, 14 NOV Mark Anderson's report of the South of Thames Junior cross country championships at Margate, where Belgrave were 3rd in the 4-man team event with Jim Estall 8th and James Ryle 10th. SOUTH OF THAMES JUN. CC CHAMPS., MARGATE, 14 NOV Mark Anderson reports:- Only seven club members made the trip to Margate for this event which was held over a flat, windy and rather tedious three lap course. All those who did compete, however, performed very well and the club was rewarded with 3rd place in the 4-man team event. Belgrave vests featured prominently at the head of the field from the start with three members amongst the leading 15 after the first mile. Roger Alsop went hard from the gun and was looking very determined as he clung to the leaders. Jim Estall was having another solid run just a few places behind Roger with James Ryle starting to move through after a cautious start. The leading two runners moved away from the rest of the field towards the end of the first circuit with a prolonged increase in pace and Roger's valiant effort was beginning to tell on him as he began to drop back on the second lap. Meanwhile, James was looking very strong as he continued his steady progress through the field and by the start of the last lap James was right behind Jim as they both worked to combat a competitive bunch vying for fifth place. In an exciting sprint finish Jim finished in 8th place with James 10th, but their placings could so easily have been two or three higher. Roger hung on well for 21st, holding off Mike Webb who had moved through to 27th to round off a solid team performance. 1, I.Hamilton (Invicta) 27:59; 2, J.Kendall (Aldershot F&D) 28:04; 3, T.Bignall (Boxhill R) 28:48; ... 8. items.s: CLUB 7.5m CC CHAMPS., WIMBLEDON COMMON, 28 NOV ARM's report of the club 7.5 mile cross country championship for the "Blackstaffe" Shield on Wimbledon Common, won by Kaessa Tadesse for his first club title, with Lionel Mann's quip and Marcello Bizio winning the handicap. CLUB 7.5m CC CHAMPS., WIMBLEDON COMMON, 28 NOV The dozen Belgravians involved in the Club Championship race for the "Blackstaffe" Shield took their places at the start line among many other runners taking part in the inter-club match to be held in conjunction but there was only ever going to be one winner of both events - Kaessa Tadesse. The young African was content to share the lead with the opposition for the first circuit, 14:03, but struck out on his own with a second of 14:08 and finished with a 13:51 to take the race by 15 seconds and with it his first club title. Our royal chef Lionel Mann was back on the Common although still limping badly from the very nasty knee injury that struck him while on a walking holiday last summer. Always one for an apt quip, the observation by an onlooker that he was not wearing a club vest earned Lionel's, "It went up in flames with everything else at Windsor Castle. Do you think I might claim for it on Ma'am's fire insurance?" Just take a minute to look at the handicap result. After three-quarters of an hour of racing Marcello scraped home by a single second from Don Anderson with Derek Clack just 6 secs. further in arrears. Well done Mr. Handicapper. items.s: REEBOK SURREY CC LEAGUE DIV. 1, RACE 3, LLOYD PARK, 9 JAN Report and results of the third Surrey League Division 1 race at Lloyd Park, where James Ryle was 16th but Belgrave again finished last (9th). REEBOK SURREY CC LEAGUE DIV. 1, RACE 3, LLOYD PARK, 9 JAN With Belgrave lying in last place in the league after the first two races Colin Pearson and other members of the committee had tried their best to persuade our middle distance stars to support the club in this important fixture. However, with injuries, work commitments and the thought of the muddy, undulating Lloyd park course, only four members of last year's twelve stage team appeared, and with Marco Mazzotta dropping out with a bad back, Andy Paton clearly unfit, and Frank Ward arriving late, it was only the ever-reliable Jim Estall of those four who performed as expected. Outstanding performance of the afternoon came from James Ryle. Improving with every race and relishing the tough conditions James had enough confidence to go off in the top dozen and he hung on well to finish 16th. One of the Arthur Bruce squad, James has shown the benefit of solid consistent winter training together with a sensible racing programme. Elsewhere, Mike Lake ran very strongly in spite of being spiked early on and Mike Webb ran his usual steady race, but only seven Belgrave runners finished in the first hundred and we finished last again on the day, nearly 200 points adrift overall. 1, V.Garner (Aldershot F&D) 27:44; 2, K.Penney (Boxhill R) 27:51; 3. items.s: CLUB 10m CC CHAMPS., WIMBLEDON COMMON, 23 JAN Light-hearted report of the club 10 mile cross country championship on Wimbledon Common, won by Marcello Bizio from Owain Lewes (who also won the handicap) and Steve Willimont, with a photo of Owain Lewes. CLUB 10m CC CHAMPS., WIMBLEDON COMMON, 23 JAN When shortly before the race Frank Ward was seen donning a pair of shoes bearing more than a trace of damp mud, it didn't really need a Sherlock Holmes to deduce that he had been hard at work on the hills of Streatham Common during the week. Was he, therefore, returning to race fitness once more? Marcello Bizio, on the other hand, was muttering about treating the event as a training run and that he didn't need a number. A suddenly officious Gordon Biscoe was all for disqualifying him there and then but had to give way when Colin Pearson announced that he had left the numbers in his car anyway and that half the field were going to have to run without one. Still, with a field of only ten, identification was not going to be a problem. Owain Lewes was looking pretty sharp and keeping quiet during all this preamble and sure enough, after two and a half miles it was his mud-streaked figure that led the field and held a clear advantage over Frank and Marcello. But unusually for this race, the order was to change at the front. Marcello took over to plough through the mud in his forceful style, Frank came out half-way through, evidently still some way from his best form, while Owain held up well to take the silver medal and romp away with the handicap result. Steve Willimont is turning into a most reliable engine-room man, turning out in successive weeks and fully deserving his "-bronze". 1, M.Bizio 59:13; 2, O.Lewes 60:21; 3, S.Willimont 63:47; 4, D.Anderson 69:22; 5, M.Graham 72:33; 6, D.McMillan 76:01; 7, R.Mann 78:32; 8, L.Mann 96:08. items.h: SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR CC CHAMPS., COULSDON, 30 JAN
items.sum: Belgrave were 6th team in the South of Thames senior cross country championships on Farthing Downs, Coulsdon, with James Ryle 11th just ahead of Frank Ward.
items.s: SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR CC CHAMPS., COULSDON, 30 JAN Belgrave were 6th team in the South of Thames senior cross country championships on Farthing Downs, Coulsdon, with James Ryle 11th just ahead of Frank Ward. SOUTH OF THAMES SENIOR CC CHAMPS., COULSDON, 30 JAN This was a far more heartening performance from the cross country team on Farthing Downs, both in terms of performance and turn out. It was a credit to Colin Pearson that he managed to get not only the twelve team members, but two travelling reserves, Trevor Williams and Tony Stone, as well. Although just missing out on the medals it is worth noting that the scoring six had less points than the previous year when we were third. It was newcomer James Ryle who again produced the best run of the day finishing in 11th position, just ahead of Frank Ward. Nice to see Frank gradually returning to fitness in time for the twelve stage. After much recent rain it was perhaps surprising to see the course fairly firm under foot apart from the muddy fields along the top of Happy Valley at the far end of the course. Two extended laps of three and a half miles with the very sharp chalky hill always proves a good test, although there are some nice flat bits as well. Belgrave got off to a good start up the long hill with Marcello Bizio in the top eight, and Frank Ward, James Ryle and Owain Lewes all in the leading twenty. At that stage the team were looking good for medals with Roger Alsop and Mike Webb packing well in the top forty. As the race progressed James managed to get up to the back of a bunch of about four which included Frank in the top dozen as they raced along the bottom of Happy Valley. Unfortunately for the team both Marcello and Owain began to slip back by the end of the first lap, Marcello suffering from stomach cramps which eventually saw him drop out of the race; with him went any chance of medals. Owain was suffering from an over ambitious start and the Club '10' the week before. James and Frank had a right ding dong battle for the remainder of the race, first one ahead and then the other until eventually, with a very strong finish, James just got the better of our Treasurer - 11th to 12th. Mike Webb finished well too, just ahead of Roger Alsop who ran a steady race to close in 35th. It was a good day for the Arthur Bruce squad who provided four runners out of the leading six and Trevor Williams, running as a guest, who had his best race for some time. 1, S.Barden (GEC) 36:40; 2, E.Hurley (F&C) 37:14; 3, S.Rayner (Hercules Wimb) 37:36; ... 11, J.Ryle 38:35; 12, F.Ward 38:38; 30, M.Webb 39:45; 35, R.Alsop 39:53; 62, C.Dickinson 40:55; 75, Mark Anderson 41:29; 81, O.Lewes 41:45; 109, S.Willimont 43:13; 110, R.Harding 43:14; 124, D.Anderson 43:39; 149, D.Clack 45:00; T.Williams also ran. items.s: SOUTH of ENGLAND CC CHAMPS., MOTE PARK, MAIDSTONE, 16 JAN South of England cross country championships at Mote Park, Maidstone, where traffic delays and injuries hit Belgrave and Mike Webb was first home in 171st. SOUTH of ENGLAND CC CHAMPS., MOTE PARK, MAIDSTONE, 16 JAN Picturesque rolling countryside, some testing inclines and a fairly stiff wind combined to make this an interesting event. Added to these elements was the uncertainty for many competitors as to whether they would even make the start line. Diversions and lengthy tailbacks heading into Maidstone resulted in many frustrated runners either still fumbling with their numbers, or launching impressive sprints towards the start line as the gun went. Most of Belgrave's top runners stayed away from the event and after one circuit of the parkland it looked as if Marcello Bizio and Marco Mazzotta wished they had as well. Marcello, having had a miserable start to the afternoon after being held up in the traffic and failing to get Kaessa Tadesse to the start line in time for the Junior event was seen walking disconsolately away from the course while Marco also came out, visibly in pain with his back trouble having flared up again. But those who finished acquitted themselves well with reliable Mike Webb our first home in 171st place. 1, D.Bannister (Shaftesbury Barnet) 48:17; 2, B.Royden (Medway) 48:40; 3, J.Freeman (Chelmsford) 48:52; ... 171, M.Webb 54:35; 324, Mike Lake 57:41; 420, D.Anderson 59:23; 473; S.Willimont 60:14; 508, R.Harding 60:56; 523, M.Anderson 61:12; 626, O.Lewes 62:51; 627. UK WORLD CC TRIALS, CORBY, 6 FEB The combined Inter-Counties and UK World Cross Country trials at Corby, where James Ryle, Belgrave's only senior man, finished 216th. INTER-COUNTIES CHAMPS., Inc. UK WORLD CC TRIALS, CORBY, 6 FEB By holding these two events together for the first time, the BAF succeeded in assembling the strongest field seen for many years in the traditional Inter-Counties race. Many more of the country's top runners represented for their counties this year hoping for a blinding run and a ticket to Amorebieta. The quality of the field was, therefore, perhaps even stronger than the first three hundred of the National. Belgrave's only senior male representative was James Ryle He found the early searing pace rather uncomfortable but held on well to finish a very creditable 216th and will benefit greatly from the experience. items.s: REEBOK SURREY LEAGUE DIV. 1, RACE 4, COULSDON, 13 FEB Final Surrey League Division 1 race at Coulsdon, won by Gary Staines with Kaessa Tadesse second; Belgrave were 4th on the day but 9th overall, with a photo of Gary Staines. REEBOK SURREY LEAGUE DIV. 1, RACE 4, COULSDON, 13 FEB At last a better performance from Belgrave in the final league fixture on Farthing Downs. Warm spring sunshine and firm conditions underfoot contrasted with the rain and mud which dominated most of the winter season and showed the Downs at their picturesque best. With Gary Staines appearing straight from warm weather training in South Africa, and most of the "engine room" present, there was a feeling before the start that Belgrave might just be able to avoid relegation. However, although Gary comfortably won the race, and Kaessa Tadesse finding the conditions much more to his liking came second, it was really a matter of too little, too late. Jim Estall returning to his best form was the only other scorer in the top twenty and with several other clubs fielding strong teams Belgrave were 4th on the day but still finished in 9th overall place in the league. Other good performances on the day came from Matt Kinane 33rd, Mike Webb 49th, and Mike Lake, who has run strongly all season, 65th. 1, G.Staines (Belgrave) 26:47; 2, K.Tadesse (Belgrave) 27:02; 3, K.Penney (Boxhill R) 27:10; 15, J.Estall 28:17; 32, M.Bizio 29:04; 33, M.Kinane 29:07; 49, M.Webb 29:33; 65, Mike Lake 30:09; 70, F.Ward 30:15; 74. items.s: CHINGFORD 5x3.5m ROAD RELAY, 13 MAR Belgrave were third in the Chingford 5x3.5m road relay, helped by Gary Staines breaking Julian Goater's 1977 lap record despite a calf injury. CHINGFORD 5x3.5m ROAD RELAY, 13 MAR Helped by a remarkable record breaking leg by Gary Staines, Belgrave achieved a very encouraging third place, ahead of notable teams such as Shaftesbury and Highgate. Gary broke the record held since 1977 by Julian Goater by six seconds in spite of pulling a calf muscle in the final 200 yards of the third leg and limping home. He had already brought the team up from 14th to 4th position. Good runs from Jim Estall and the ever improving Roger Alsop on the last two legs moved Belgrave through to a well earned third place. 1, London Irish 83:19; 2, Woodford Green 84:06; 3, Belgrave (M.Mazzotta 17:30, O.Lewes 17:55, G.Staines 15:43, J.Estall 16:58, R.Alsop 16:49) 84:58; ... dnf Belgrave 'B' (R.Harding 18:51, Mark Anderson 17:55, T.Williams 20:20, J.Galley 17:54). items.s: BELGRAVE HALF-MARATHON, WIMBLEDON, 14 MAR The first Belgrave Half Marathon at Wimbledon, organised by John Wasbrough, won by New Zealander Alistair Miller with Marcello Bizio 2nd and Helen Maskrey winning the ladies' race, with Ray Xerri's photo of the start. BELGRAVE HALF-MARATHON, WIMBLEDON, 14 MAR The first Belgrave Half Marathon held over a course similar to the old Belgrave '20' produced a good quality field and some respectable times. The race was organised very well by John Wasbrough and now looks set to become an annual event. There were some excellent prizes, the course was well marshalled, and although the number of competitors was not great there was good support from Belgrave and Hercules Wimbledon members. Three runners almost immediately broke away from the field - two from H/W and our own Marcello Bizio. By the end of the first trip along the by-pass it was down to two - the very strong New Zealander Alistair Miller and the Belgravian - but the pair were soon split asunder by the first ascent of Copse Hill. The Kiwi continued to go away on the second circuit and eventually came home in 68:02, a good time on a course that includes two climbs of 'Copse'. Marcello remained in 2nd with 69:29 ahead of another H/W man Steve Stockwell. Helen Maskrey had the best Belgrave run of the day winning the Ladies race in 82:07 and breaking her PB for the distance. 1, A.Miller (Hercules Wimb) 1:08:02; 2, M.Bizio (Belgrave) 1:09:29; 3, S.Stockwell (Hercules Wimb) 1:10:49; ... 16, H.Maskrey (1st Woman) 1:22:07; 19, C.Taplin 1:23:25; 22, M.Graham 1:24:19; 26, A.Stone 1:26:44; 33, R.Mann 1:29:13. items.s: READING HALF-MARATHON, 28 MAR Paul Evans won the Reading Half-Marathon in 1:01:38, over two minutes clear, breaking the course record by 29 seconds. READING HALF-MARATHON, 28 MAR With three weeks to the London Marathon, Paul Evans blasted a spectacular warning to his rivals when he visited the Berkshire town of Reading. It might have only been a "half-marathon" but this man never does things by halves. The field included several Russians and Kenyans plus some of Britain's best road runners yet the Belgravian came home over two minutes clear in 1:01:38, a time exactly equalling his Great North Run clocking. A brutal third mile of 4:39 put paid to the hopes of the majority in the lead pack but this paled into insignificance when Paul let rip with an astounding 13:37 three miles from the six to eight mile markers! Now well clear he continued pouring on the effort and ended up smashing the six year-old course record by 29 seconds. items.h: Bels raise their game for Southern Road Relay
items.sum: Report of the South of England 12-stage road relay at Thurrock, where a depleted Belgrave team managed by Colin Pearson finished 11th (10th after Hounslow's disqualification) to qualify for the National Road Relay.
items.s: Bels raise their game for Southern Road Relay Report of the South of England 12-stage road relay at Thurrock, where a depleted Belgrave team managed by Colin Pearson finished 11th (10th after Hounslow's disqualification) to qualify for the National Road Relay. Bels raise their game for Southern Road Relay SOUTH OF ENGLAND 12-STAGE ROAD RELAY, THURROCK, 4 APR Perhaps 11th position may not seem much after the glories and past triumphs in the old London to Brighton and then the Belgrave 12-Stage, but this was a magnificent performance by a team decimated by illness, injuries and withdrawals. It is a tribute to team manager Colin Pearson that he managed not only to put together a team, but one which finished high enough to qualify for the National Road Relay and in doing so beat all our rivals from the Surrey League except Boxhill, who won, and Hounslow, who only came by us after Marco Mazzotta went off course. Throughout the afternoon, Colin's cheerful confidence spread throughout the team, half of whom were unfit, or in the case of Marcello Bizio, actually ill. He had got out of his sick bed to run. We were without Evans, Staines, Foote and Paton but it didn't matter. There was John Gladwin running in the same team as his old friend Mark Sinclair for the first time in years, the pair of them enjoying themselves and the occasion. And several others were given the chance to represent Belgrave and they ran above themselves for their club. Of course the occasion was not like Wimbledon. The relay has been moved from our home patch because of ever increasing problems with the traffic: here the changeover was just in front of the main stand of a small running track set in the heart of a bleak part of Essex. After the gun it was half a lap of the track, then out through a housing estate and past a handful of spectators, down a narrow, straight, flat country lane and off into the distance. Five minutes later the crocodile of runners could just be seen as they ran up the incline of the bridge over the busy Southend road. Yes, it was Giovanni Rizzo ahead, silhouetted against the electric pylons and A13 traffic a mile away. Then, not a sight of them until they returned to negotiate a nasty cross road threequarters of a mile from the finish, one which later in the day had short and long stage runners coming and going in three directions, tempers fraying, motorists honking, marshals becoming frantic - a scene all so familiar. Thurrock were learning what putting on a road relay was all about. Boxhill led at the end of the first stage, a position they were never to lose, with Belgrave's Roger Alsop, running so well at the moment, just on 25 minutes in 24th place. Owain Lewes, who is aiming for a season of shorter track races, showed the benefit of recent speed work with one of his best runs for the club on the next short stage. On leg three, Jim Estall produced his usual reliable run in spite of high mileage marathon training: "Can't I run two legs ?" Then a half fit Frank Ward got round on memory to hand over to Steve Halliday, down from Halifax for the race, as cheery as ever and having a blinding run with 4th fastest long stage of the day to move Belgrave up from 17th to 10th. Progression continued with John Gladwin, again only half fit, on the next short stage, and handing on to Kaessa Tadesse who had the difficult task of setting out just behind a bunch containing Andy Bristow and Dominic Bannister, the Southern champion. Bristow ran a time second only to Eammon Martin's fastest of the day but Kaessa also ran an excellent leg and broke Bannister 1.5 miles from the finish. Mark Sinclair ran even faster than John Gladwin, passing on to Mike Webb, rather happier on the country but as reliable as ever. Then a buoyant Darrell Maynard was a second faster than Mark. Poor Marco Mazzotta, not really fit enough for a long stage, but willing to fill in for Marcello who had been ill all week with a tooth abscess and 'flu. Marco took a wrong turning, lost at least a minute, and then ran himself to exhaustion trying to make up for it. This left Marcello on the last leg, could he maintain 11th position and qualify the team for Sutton Park later in the month. Of course the answer was yes. When ever did Marcello let the team down in a situation like this. He ran with fire in his eyes and produced the team's fastest short stage, just ducking under 14 minutes. In the end there was just over a minute between the leading three teams but the chasers never really got close to Boxhill who seemed to be about the only team at full strength. No, it didn't have the same atmosphere as Wimbledon, let alone the London to Brighton, but it was an enjoyable and successful day for Belgrave nevertheless. 1, Boxhill 3:47:37; 2, Southampton 3:48:14; 3, London Irish 3:48:57; ... 11, Belgrave (R.Alsop 25:00, O.Lewes 14:29, J.Estall 24:51, F.Ward 14:21, S.Halliday 23:39, J.Gladwin 14:12, K.Tadesse 24:04, M.Sinclair 14:04, M.Webb 26:35, D.Maynard 14:03, M.Mazzotta 27:56, M.Bizio 13:59) 3:57:13; 57 teams finished. items.sum: Account of the 1993 London Marathon seen from Tower Bridge, where favourite Paul Evans, suffering from a sore throat, dropped out; Jim Estall was 89th and E. Martin of Basildon won.
items.s: THE LONDON MARATHON, 18 APR Account of the 1993 London Marathon seen from Tower Bridge, where favourite Paul Evans, suffering from a sore throat, dropped out; Jim Estall was 89th and E. Martin of Basildon won. THE LONDON MARATHON, 18 APR After Paul Evans' exciting 1992 season which included, of course, his fine 5th place in last year's 'London', he was most people's favourite to sweep up the honours in this year's edition of the classic. He had raced sparingly in the run-up to the event yet destroyed the field when he had ventured out in his racing kit. But we know so well that there is no such thing as a certainty in athletics where a very fine line divides the super-fit from those suffering injury or illness. Unknown to us spectators, Paul had started suffering from a sore throat on the Saturday afternoon but come the morning of the race, he was still intent on competing. At the 'House on the Bridge', a bar on the southern approach to Tower Bridge nearing the 13 mile point, a television visible from the pavement had thoughtfully been left switched on overnight; no doubt the licensee was hoping to attract the marathon crowd when he opened later in the day. At 9.30am, like moths gathered around a candle flame, athletics fans were shoulder to shoulder on the footpath outside, noses pressed against the bar window to watch the initial stages of the race. At the early mile markers Paul could be seen in the leading pack but with the women's race due along soon it was time to desert the TV and take up a place at the barriers. Nothing matches actually being present at a big sporting occasion. We had been warmed up by the wheelchair competitors, the Liz and Lisa show had moved on past, and now, with the energy of a tide in full flood, the leaders in the men's field, a group some thirty strong, burst around the corner from Abbey Street into Tower Bridge Road with the accompanying cheering and flag waving from the watchers being pushed along ahead of them like so much flotsam. Where was Paul? There - no that's the tall blonde Polish runner. What could have happened. Jim Estall came by and cheerfully waved back on hearing his name called. Some hundreds of runners streamed through before Evans was sighted, a mere shadow of his normal self and, to be honest, looking quite unwell. He came out somewhere over the bridge and must have been bitterly disappointed to leave the race in the hands of those he had previously been confident of beating. Nevertheless, he has already been selected for the World Champs. in Stuttgart and if he can pop out that 2:08 effort then, without the prior warning of 'London', it's going to cause an even greater shock. 1, E.Martin (Basildon) 2:10:50; 2, I.Rico (Mexico) 2:10:53; 3, G.Gadjus (Poland) 2:11:07; ... 89, J.Estall 2:28:44; 1345, J.Galley 2:57:11; 1403, A.Verdie 2:57:43 ... further positions in the next edition. items.h: NATIONAL 12-STAGE ROAD RELAY, SUTTON PARK, 24 APR
items.sum: Report of the National 12-stage road relay at Sutton Park, won by Shaftesbury Barnet, with an illness-hit Belgrave 35th, Steve Halliday going off course while leading the first stage.
items.s: NATIONAL 12-STAGE ROAD RELAY, SUTTON PARK, 24 APR Report of the National 12-stage road relay at Sutton Park, won by Shaftesbury Barnet, with an illness-hit Belgrave 35th, Steve Halliday going off course while leading the first stage. NATIONAL 12-STAGE ROAD RELAY, SUTTON PARK, 24 APR It was in 1974 that the National Road Relay was held for the first time at Sutton Park and there have been some impressive runs by individuals and teams throughout the intervening years. This year the winning time was well outside the top ten but for excitement it was second to none. The Midland clubs, who hold their area championship on the same course, were strongly tipped to provide the medallists but when it came to the 'cards down' it was the South that held the aces. The Shaftesbury Barnet team manager judged things just right, for John Sherban, on the penultimate leg, set the fastest long stage time of the day in turning a 30 second deficit into a 55 second lead. And then the thrills continued with Boxhill Racers, through Tom Bignall, moving from outside the frame into 2nd spot on the very last lap while Swansea's tail-end super-vets held the chasing hordes at bay for 3rd. The Belgrave outfit was again hit by illness and injury with young Marlon Anderson getting pretty close to the action as next on the reserve list. Stage 1 was taken by Steve Halliday who was most certainly on for one of the fastest times of the day - except that while holding a 70 yard lead over the field he went off course, lost about a minute, and then trailed in a disconsolate 18th! Our fastest short stage came from Roger Alsop on leg 2. He covered the 3m 8y in 14:40 to retrieve three places and, bearing in mind the gradients, set a time which must equate to about 15 minutes for 5,000m, a target he surely must achieve before too long. Kaessa Tadesse was the pick of the rest of our long stage runners, benefiting from Steve's misfortune to become our fastest over the 5m 706y stretch with 26:06, and Johnny G took yet another step along the road to fitness by running a 14:50 effort that makes an appearance over 800m in our team for Budapest begin to look a real possibility. 1, Shaftesbury Barnet 4:06:24; 2, Boxhill Racers 4:07:01; 3, Swansea 4:07:07; ... 35, Belgrave 4:20:42. items.sum: Editorial reviewing Belgrave's 1993 across cross country, road, track and field, walking, young athletes and veterans, including the European Clubs' Cup in Budapest and John Regis's World Championships silver.
items.s: Editorial reviewing Belgrave's 1993 across cross country, road, track and field, walking, young athletes and veterans, including the European Clubs' Cup in Budapest and John Regis's World Championships silver. At the time of writing it is touch and go whether this magazine will be with you by the New Year but at any rate, it will not be far behind. It's a quiet time of the year. The big road and cross-country events are a little way off yet and the coming warmth of the track season is just beyond the horizon. No doubt you will be able to find a peaceful hour or two after training's been done for the day so why not sit back in the armchair before the fire, a noggin of your favourite brew near to hand and spend a little time with "The Belgravian". Reflect upon what 1993 brought us and consider what 1994 has in store. In men's cross country things looked a little sad for us as we came out of last winter. Kasse Tadesse gave us a silver medal in the National Junior CC Champs. but we were relegated to the second division in our league. Our ladies, however, took great delight in fighting their way up their league and already this winter they have shaken the opposition in Surrey Division One. They were not far from winning their opening two league fixtures, placed highly in the Southern Road Relay and then just before Christmas delighted us with their first ever Women's Surrey County Cross-Country Championship win. The new season has also brought a surge of enthusiasm to our male cross country runners. It will be a while before we attain the heights of years gone by - these things go in cycles - but we surely will regain Surrey Division One status before the winter is over and we are on our way. On the road, as on the country, our women's team are beginning to make a name for themselves and individually, with Kasse, Paul Evans and a resurgent Gary Staines, we have men who are among the very best in the nation over all events from 10k to the marathon. Could we possibly, just once, get them all out in the same race? Nineteen ninety-three brought us another superb season in track and field although our men's first team were unable to maintain the extraordinarily high standard set the previous summer due to injuries and fixtures clashing with international events, robbing us of our top men. We ended up second to Haringey in the GRE Gold Cup Competition - ten points more and that gold trophy would have been ours for all time as third-time consecutive winners. We were also beaten by the men from North London in the British League. Our second and third teams remained steady in their area leagues and Bob Bridge's dream of being the first British League club to have their second team win Division One of the Southern League is not impossible. A first for us was the honour of representing the United Kingdom in the European Clubs' Cup in Budapest. We learned a lot in Hungary: how truly professional some of the European clubs are, how tough we must be as team managers and athletes to secure every single available point - and how to get ripped off in the street by Eastern European currency swindlers! Six of our members were selected to represent Britain in the World Championships and of these John Regis consistently had the name "Belgrave Harriers" on the commentators' lips as he collected the 200 metres silver medal and British Record. Only one man on the globe has more World Championship medals to his name than John: that man is Carl Lewis. Another fourteen or fifteen of our men competed at international level. The world of Women's Track & Field at club level is different to the men's. Here all age groups score in the same match. Although our seniors did the business with spear and spikes and would have carried the day on their own, our shortage of girls in the younger age group meant a lack of points that we could not overcome. Nevertheless, we held our own in Southern League Division Three and are still poised for advancement. We watch with interest as it now looks as though competitions are soon to be organised along the same lines as the men's, with senior competitors scoring separately from the youngsters. The enthusiasm of our women's team is epitomised by the keenness with which they have taken to the new events available - pole vault and triple jump. In the words of our leading walker, "the walking scene has been very quiet for us." Problems with rule interpretations differing from one nation to another and a corresponding lack of success by Britain at international level has led to a decline in the sport in this country. Belgrave have suffered as much as most. What can we do to bring this branch of our sport back into fashion? Our young male athletes are on the verge of running riot. It's a difficult thing to maintain annual team progress when each season sees a flow of athletes out of the top of the age group and into the next but we have done it. Thanks to very hard work by coaches and team managers we have consolidated our position in the Southern Premier League and as some of our leading Youths become Juniors next summer you may be sure that our under-20 team is about to take off in a big way. No fewer than nine Belgrave Girls and Boys represented their counties in the All-England Schools and we had two winners. We now have track & field from the cradle to the grave, for at the other end of the age spectrum we entered the Southern Veteran's T&F League for the first time. Not only did we place 3rd in our division in both women's and men's competitions but we did manage to teach old dogs new tricks to such good effect that the regular teams benefited as a result. However, one of the most exciting things to come out of 1993 has been the will of our membership to consider radical ways of improving all aspects of our Club life. Every Club worker is looking for ideas in our quest to make Belgrave the greatest all round team in the world of athletics. Nothing is being thrown out as "impossible". items.s: Newsletter of the Belgrave Hall & Social Committee Derek Manning, secretary of the new Hall and Social Management Committee, sets out plans to refurbish Belgrave Hall and lists 1994 social events and committee contacts. NEWSLETTER of the Belgrave Hall & Social Committee As you are no doubt aware, there has been a change in the management structure of the club as a result of which a new Hall and Social Management Committee was formed. I was elected to sit as its secretary and therefore I would like to explain, very briefly, what I would like to see achieved for you, the members. Firstly the repair and refurbishment of both the ladies and gents showers, toilets, and changing rooms. Then I would like to provide, not only a well equipped gymnasium, but a gymnasium that would be a pleasure to 'work out' in and that could be used by all members of the club at any time of day or evening. I would also like to see the bar and kitchen facilities upgraded so that they represent a venue to which members would like to come, to drink and eat in, and bring their friends to with a degree of pride. What I don't want to do is lose the identity and atmosphere of an athletic club operating for the benefit of its athletes and their friends. I appreciate that this a fairly ambitious programme, but, with the help of my committee members and yourselves it can be achieved. Imagine that the gymnasium has been completely refurbished and the bar and kitchen upgraded to a high degree, the toilets, showers and changing rooms have been renovated and everything looks smart. Once that has been completed, I'm sure one of our qualified members would consider running fitness classes for various groups of people, not only club members, but persons who could become associate members, or corporate members, and the same would apply to any member of the club wanting to start up aerobic and other types of classes. If the venue looked the part, there was a nice bar area to sit and relax in and possibly get a drink or a meal, then I believe the Hall and Social Club could become the main source of income for the benefit of our athletes and our promotion of athletics. Obviously all of this will take time and money to achieve, And that's where you can help by attending the various social events being arranged. For the time being make a note of the following dates and try to support the events by coming along and spending some of your hard earned cash. It's your money I want. Sun 23rd Jan 1994 Eat in with Marcello Sat 12th Feb 1994 Valentine Disco, £3.50 Sat 19th Mar 1994 Horse Racing Evening Sun 10th Apr 1994 Eat in with Marcello Sat 14th May 1994 Barn Dance Sat 18th Jun 1994 Caribbean Evening * *Dress optional , but it has to be tropical or pay a fine I need a venue during July or August for a Barbecue or fun evening. Has anyone got a suitable site we can use? The annual Dinner Dance has been provisionally arranged for Saturday 12th November 1994 at the same venue as for 1993 where everyone who went had a great time. Reserve the date please. Some of you will no doubt have ideas of your own for an evening's entertainment. Let's have them and we will try to arrange them, with your own help if you like. Anyone who wishes to hire the Hall can do so by ringing Derek Crookes, the Hall bookings manager, or any other member of the committee listed below who will be pleased to help in any way they can. items.s: County Cross-Country Champs Report of the Surrey County Cross-Country Championships at Frimley, where Belgrave won four sets of team medals including the club's first ever senior women's team title; the photo caption names "Martin Ryan" where the report has Martina (M.Ryan). COUNTY CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPS It was cold - it was windy; but the trip to Frimley to watch the Surrey County Cross-Country Championships was well worth while from the Belgrave point of view. No fewer than four sets of team medals came our way and pride of place must go to our Senior Women's team who gave us our first ever women's cross-country team title. Clear a space on that honours board! All the races started with a 200 metre dash across the playing fields and by the time the runners disappeared up a steep, narrow climb into the murky pine woods, claret and gold was already a predominant colour at the front of the pack, along with the red and black of Herne Hill. On completion of the first circuit Woking's Zara Hyde, a regular winner in recent years and just back from road racing in the USA, was making a strong bid to break away from the field. As that oh! so steep climb up through the woods was tackled for the first time she had achieved her aim - apart from the fact that Gabrielle Collison was giving all she had to hang on, 15 metres in arrears. Remember, Gabby was 17th last year! These two were clear but when the main field arrived we were thrilled to find Martina First ever team title for Belgrave Women Ryan and Helen Maskrey both well inside the first ten, racing each other neck and neck with Martina just showing ahead. Then there was Jacinta Moore fighting her way up the sandy climb in the twenties. The positions were now more or less established and by the second time up the hill the Woking girl was beyond Gabby's sight but she, in turn, was miles ahead of the rest. Somewhere on that circuit Helen had got ahead of her team-mate but Martina wasn't giving up in a hurry and was slugging along close behind. And that's the way they finished. Last year we were disappointed to miss out on the bronze medals when Herne Hill ran out winners. This year they scored even less points but the Bels. were devastating, getting our scoring three home in the first eight to take gold. Our Under 15 Boys had started the medal spree by gaining an unexpected second team place, both Simon Alexander and James Drake running very confidently. The Under 17 trophy had more or less been expected to come our way but as the race got under way we were without our number one man Matt Hillier. Gavin Mason, just over the 'flu', and Adam Jones led the team throughout with Toby Earle running a 'blinder', hitting that hill as if he was having his own personal battle with the elements. As the runners entered the playing fields for the final 600 metres Gavin switched up into hyper-drive to tear away from his rival from Epsom & Ewell, Gavin Russell, and place 5th. With four to score, the remainder of our team came down the steep drop to the fields together. Toby was now running like a madman, leaping the last ten feet of the drop, chasing Adam for all he was worth and trying to keep ahead of our fourth man Scott Walsh. Great running! Incidentally, Scott was entered incorrectly as Scott West - which must have made one or two wonder how we had signed up one of the nation's leading young runners. Our Scott has swum competitively for years and picked up a few prizes, but here he was only a few weeks into his athletic career and picking up a Surrey team winner's medal. With a 2:19 marathon in his legs Kasse Tadesse appeared to be taking the 5 mile Junior race very comfortably, loping along behind Mole Valley's Bruno Witchells. And lo and behold! there was Matt Hillier, just behind them and racing without a number. Poor old Matt had been stuck in a delayed train for three-quarters of an hour. He'd missed the Youths race and was unable (officially) to contest the Junior one. Kasse and Bruno were still together in the last quarter-mile and one might have expected Witchells' 1:52 800m speed to have given him the edge as they approached the finish. Not a bit of it. Kasse must have a 49 second 400m in him the way he toured that field. Matt came towards the finishing funnel in fourth place - and then startled the crowd by veering to the wrong side to avoid the final line. He is in great form and must have had a fine chance of winning the Under 17 event. Happily the officials will still consider him for the Inter-County race. Great backing by Marlon Anderson, Stuart Booth and Martin Readhead - and another set of team winners medals were ours. Our Seniors, too, ran well, with Graham Adams leading the boys home. Roger Alsop might have been expected to have made the first ten but it's noticeable that on a course like this, with a narrow climb soon after the start, one has to commit one's self early. "Rodg" seems to prefer to come through as the race progresses but here, the leaders had got too far away by then. items.s: County CC Stats Historical notes on Belgrave's record in the Surrey County Cross-Country Championships, mentioning Gerry North, Pam Davies, Jon Dennis and John Gladwin. COUNTY CC STATS It's 26 years since our senior men last won the Surrey Cross-Country Championship - 1967 when our Captain Gerry North took the second of his four consecutive individual titles. The individual winner of the Surrey Women's Championship takes home a silver cup which was presented to the County by our own Pam Davies, herself the individual winner (in the colours of Selsonia) on no fewer than seven occasions, six of them being consecutive between 1962 and 1967. The last time we won a team title of any sort was in 1988 at Coulsdon - the Junior race, which coincidentally was won by Jon Dennis of Camberley and now a Belgravian. Our last individual winner in any age group was John Gladwin - 1987 at Camberley. John was at this year's race, jogging the course before his operation due the following week. We have had individual winners in every male age group except the under 13s. items.s: Sidetracked Club gossip column: an old member "Jack" Frost, Tom Carter's 1946 British Games programme, Derek Burfitt's 1946 Youths 880yds win, two English Schools champions, Gerry North managing a veterans' team, and John Davies's old Onitsuka shoes. Sidetracked • Marianne and Alan Black were accosted at the Harry Hawks '8' by a jovial old gent who, upon spotting Alan's club singlet, said that he used to belong to Belgrave many years ago. "Jack" Frost was his name and some time was idly spent as each party went through the routine of coming up with names that belonged to possible mutual acquaintances. One name that soon entered the conversation was, of course, that of Tom Carter, remembered very well by Mr. Frost. "Jack" passes on his best wishes to all at the Club who remember him. • Coincidentally, our Tom had been rummaging through his loft again and only a couple of days later, without any fore-knowledge, brought up to the Hall an old British Games programme dating back to Whit Monday, 1946. On the page for Event 23, the Open Three Miles Scratch Race, was a list of competitors headed by photographs of the area champions, including Tom. Alongside Tom's name in the entry list were those of J. Smart, T. Clinton and L. Herbert, all Belgrave, S.Belton of Surrey AC, ... and A. Frost, also Belgrave. • Among the events held on that long gone Whit Monday was an 880yds event for Youths. Sixty-six young men had entered, and just 45 minutes after the first of the five heats was started, the final was won by Belgravian Derek Burfitt. Youths in those days were those who were between their 17th and 19th birthdays. What would they have thought of today's Youths, under 17 and turning out times in the mid 1:50s. Which of course takes us on nicely to ... • Our two English Schools Champions. We have had ESAA winners before but they have been few and far between. How pleased we are then to have two winners from this year's meeting. Gavin Mason took the under-17 800 metres, drawing to within striking distance of John Gladwin's Club record, while James Hilston set new under-15 figures for the 400 metres, breaking a record that has stood for 32 years. Great running by both, at a meeting where we had no less than nine youngsters in action. • From one end of the age spectrum to the other. At the Southern Veterans T&F League Final where our men and women were representing Mid-London a familiar face was spotted managing the Hampshire and Mid-Surrey Ladies' Team - Gerry North. Our Captain and Cross-Country Champion from the 60s was looking very well indeed and there was much rivalry throughout the day as he urged his girls to "duff ours up". Unfortunately Gerry does no running at all these days - although you wouldn't think so to look at him. Severe knee trouble has brought him to a halt, the legacy of one hundred miles a week training, year in and year out, in shoes that had almost nothing in the way of cushioning and support. • And talking of such shoes ... John Davies dug out a pair that he has had tucked away these last thirty years, a pair of Onitsuka "Tiger Cubs". They were in almost new condition - white canvas with the red and blue pattern support that we now know as the Asics trademark and a sole surely no more than 5mm thick. At the time they were a revolution: a marathon shoe as light as a feather and costing only 27s 6d (£1.37) at a time when an Adidas racing shoe would have been around £10-£15. John handed them over to Alan Black who was actually thinking of taking a trip down memory lane and running in them - which is just about where we came in. Wheelchair Athlete competes for Belgrave It is with pleasure that we welcome Matthew Coleman as an Honorary member. He is the first "Wheelchair Athlete" to wear Belgrave colours. Competing on the road in 1993 he has had several fine races: 1st St. Ives 10kms, 2nd St. Neots Fun Run and three gold medals at the Blackpool races. Also this year he has been participating in the GRE Grand Prix meetings run in conjunction with the British Track & Field Championships, qualifying for the Grand Prix Finals at Bedford. Our congratulations to Matthew on these splendid performances, remarkable when one realises that he only commenced the sport in January of this year. We wish him every success in the future. items.s: One track mind Poem "Just Ten" by sprinter Ernest Obeng contrasting a spectator's view of a 100m race with the athlete's years of effort. One track mind - a Runner's Primer of Poetry by Ernest Obeng Just Ten To you it's just ten seconds; To me it's been five years. To you it's just a 100 dash; To me it's sweat and tears. To you it's just the gun then run; To me it's skills, technique. To you it's raw aggression, strength: To me it's power and peak. To you it's just dive for the tape: To me it's body lean. To you it's over far too soon; To me it's long and mean. To you these men of varied sizes And shapes crouched on one knee Might just as well be saying prayers, But who says prayers for me? Published with Ernie's kind permission Ernest Obeng Ernest Obeng Ernest Obeng Ernie

items.s: From The Belgravian "From the Belgravian" column recalling Alf Harley's 1943 fantasy of the club in 1960 and December 1968 news of Derek Boosey's Olympic selection. FROM THE BELGRAVIAN 50 YEARS AGO ..... October 1943 A Flight of Fancy? In a fantasy article looking 17 years into the future, to 1960, Alf Harley predicted the following, with tongue in cheek no doubt! "As I look down on the swirl of traffic which flows Eastwards thro' Hyde Park towards the new double-cross-over traffic bridge at Piccadilly Circus ... I ponder on the position Belgrave Harriers have now attained ... I am sitting in one of the offices devoted to the production of "The Belgravian", lavishly illustrated these days and published weekly, and recognised as the leading authority on all matters concerning athletics. These offices form part of the magnificent building in Knightsbridge which houses The Club's Town Headquarters and preserves its associations with the City of Westminster, and from which training takes place most evenings over Rotten Row. At Wimbledon the Belgrave Harriers still have their week-end headquarters, now situated on Common Side; and every Saturday thro'out the Winter hundreds of athletes in the familiar claret and gold enjoy their favourite sport on the neighbouring roads and common land .... ..... The Committee realises that the facilities the Club can now offer, which are unrivalled anywhere in the World, might well attract a type of member who was merely interested in its restaurant, billiard room and luxurious lounges, but with no interests in running, walking or field events; and so all members are called upon during their first ten years of membership to make at least twenty appearances in athletic races or competitions each year ..... " 25 YEARS AGO ..... December 1968 "Our congratulations go to Derek Boosey who has been selected to represent Great Britain in the triple jump at the Mexico Olympic Games. He partners Fred Alsop who was 4th at Tokyo in 1964. Another to tread that lonely Tartan strip will be our second-claim long-jumper Alan Lerwill, who is coached by our own Dave Ansell. We wish them both every success. Our sympathies go to John Thresher and Ray Middleton who narrowly missed selection for the 5,000 metres and 50km walk respectively. items.h: Two champions for Bels at All-England Schools
items.sum: Report and results of the All-England Schools Championships at Blackpool, where James Hilston and Gavin Mason won titles and several Belgrave club records fell.
items.s: Two champions for Bels at All-England Schools Report and results of the All-England Schools Championships at Blackpool, where James Hilston and Gavin Mason won titles and several Belgrave club records fell. Two champions for Bels at All-England Schools BLACKPOOL, 9/10 JUL Never before have we had nine competitors in the All-England Schools and never before have we had two winners. It really is a tribute to our coaches that our youngsters are beginning to take the athletic world by storm. Pride of place goes to our two champions James Hilston and Gavin Mason. James coolly took 2nd place in his opening round of the Junior 400m, setting a personal best, and the semi also saw him giving little away to the opposition with a 3rd place in yet another best. Come the final though, the wraps came off in earnest as the Belgrave lad hit the opposition hard in taking another full second off his best and gaining a resounding victory and Club Record. That record, incidentally, has stood since 1961, set by Roger Hudson who won this very same title in that year. Gavin Mason was unable to take our Youths' Club Record as he too set personal bests in heat and final of the Intermediate 800m - but he wasn't far off and one has to remember that John Gladwin hasn't made it easy for those that follow in his footsteps. Gavin's first heat win was matched by arch-rival and Surrey team-mate Toby Dolman in heat three and the final was eagerly anticipated. Would Surrey Champion Dolman get the better of the Belgravian again? No fear! Gavin is now developing a keen racing brain, staying closer to the action throughout. This time there was no mistake as our man kept with the leader, struck at 200 to go as the other man dropped out, was then overtaken by Dolman but came again and kept a couple of metres of daylight between them to the line. Both went under 1:56 for the first time. Another record came from Jessica Dash in the "inter" 300 hurdles. The mark was her own property already - 46.77 set in last year's English Schools - and here she chopped a huge chunk off in progressing to the final. Her London colleague Natasha Danvers blew the opposition away with an unbelievable 41.99 but Jessica went inside her old best again to run home 7th. Incredibly, Ben Cascoe is throwing further this year with the 700 and 800gm spears than he did last year with the 600gm implement. He was only 3 metres behind the winner and will be in the same age group next year. Sprint hurdlers Mellisa Simon and Steve Scott were both held back by the gusting wind but Marlon Dickson and Daniel Jackman were able to use it to their advantage. Both ran fast times with Marlon, who picked up a medal as one of London's 4x100m squad, reaching the final of the shorter event. Both of Daniel's 200m runs took him below the best time ever recorded by a Belgrave U15 but those wind readings over 2mps following mean that he cannot call the new mark truly his own. As no wind speed readings are known for Clive Gardner's 1983 mark the best that we can do is keep both of them on the record books. Yet another Belgrave best came from Rob Milner. Even so, he was a little unfortunate as his heat time of 57.31, 8th fastest in the whole of the first round, placed him only 3rd in his race and he had to be content with a performance which erased Alasdair Grant's name from the list. items.h: Profile of a President - Alan Mead
items.sum: Clive Shippen's profile of new club President Alan Mead: joining Belgrave in 1958, his club roles and editorships, Police and Australian years, Morris dancing, and his part in restructuring the club with wife Pat and daughter Hazel.
items.s: Profile of a President - Alan Mead Clive Shippen's profile of new club President Alan Mead: joining Belgrave in 1958, his club roles and editorships, Police and Australian years, Morris dancing, and his part in restructuring the club with wife Pat and daughter Hazel. Profile of a President - Alan Mead Clive Shippen writes about our President for 1993-94 It was 35 years ago, in 1958, that a fourteen years old youth stepped gingerly through the portals of Belgrave Hall and found it "awe inspiring". The Hall, with its then open interior, exuded an odour of perspiration, liniment and old shoes; and the figures of Alf Harley and Bill Webb effused an almost religious aura as they greeted the newcomer with a warmth and interest he has never forgotten. When Alan Mead read Bill Webb's letter of welcome, a letter he preserved for many years, he never dreamt that one day he would become President of this "awe inspiring" Club. It just goes to show that there's a President's medal waiting to emerge from the pack of every youth. Much commitment and enthusiasm is necessary of course, but Alan is not short of those qualities. He has used them in a whole range of Club appointments, covering captaincy, secretarial, managerial and journalistic positions. His present post as co-editor of "The Belgravian" is his third stint, totalling 15 years of magazine production. Thirty-five years ago at Beverley School none of this was further from Alan's mind until, much to his surprise, he won a school race. His teachers were closely allied to Surrey AC and were keen to encourage him in that direction, but a stronger draw was Hercules AC where his father had run competitively for several years. However, Belgrave's history stepped in to provide a third alternative. A fellow-pupil revealed that his own father and grandfather (a former mayor of New Malden) had belonged to a famous club who actually had a trophy named after his aunt Elsie. It sounded a tall story, particularly when the Club was revealed to be Belgrave Harriers; but in fact his grandfather was none other than Past President Teddy Gordon. Alan was impressed. So too were a couple of other class-mates, Dave Cocks and John Jarvis. All four decided to join Belgrave; Doug Gordon dropping out fairly soon but Dave Cocks going on to be a Surrey County 880 yards Champion with a sub 1:50 performance. Alan remembers those early years for the organisation of a young athletes section by Tom Carter and then by Jack Hampshire. Tom led the pack round the horse rides of Wimbledon Common on Tuesday and Thursday evenings making sure that none of the difficult parts were missed out. Alan found it tough on that surface, and as the pack got fitter he found it tougher still. His attributes were really at the sprinting end of the spectrum, but Belgrave Hall in those days was full of runners and walkers. The steamy atmosphere on Winter Saturdays strangely attracted him. In 1967, after spells at Westminster Bank and the Welbecson Press in Battersea, he joined the Police. Training school made him fitter than ever and he gained great satisfaction from winning the school's cross-country championships, and then leading the team in the inter-divisional championships. He was posted to Clapham Police Station, the station of Belgrave's international Brian Morris, and he soon got to know John Jeffrey of the Balham branch, future England team manager and Belgravian. Third place in the British Police Championships 400m behind international Chris Carter gave him great satisfaction and he now came under the eagle eye of Andy Norman, then manager of the Police team. Norman was a demanding team manager and Alan doubled up at fixtures with a string of sub 51.0 and sub 2:00 performances. On one occasion he was required to run a 400 hurdles as well and was accused of not trying hard enough. Alan smiles wryly at the memory. He smiles too at an incident that occurred during one of the protest rallies of those days. Weekend after weekend had been spent outside the US Embassy in Grosvenor Square when he was part of a police barrier keeping back anti-Vietnam War protesters. Among the mob at the conclusion of one of these demonstrations, in Hyde Park, was Belgravian team-mate Chris Steer. As Alan and Chris communed together about this bizarre encounter, Chris was being angrily eyed up for "talking to that pig" while Alan was being rebuked for fraternising with "that long-haired layabout". Perhaps there's a moral there somewhere. The Police was his third attempt at a career but that too did not give him the satisfaction he sought. On a succession of nights in the bitter winter of 1968/69 he was posted to the rear of Brixton Prison to help thwart a proposed attempt to spring the Kray brothers. Hours of solitude, darkness and bitterly cold weather was a great stimulus for thought, and it did not require much of it to make Australia seem paradise. His feet began to itch once more and in 1969 he and Pat left for that far land. All of this time he had taken a great interest in Club affairs. There are no half measures with Alan; it's all or nothing. He had been elected Junior Captain in 1962 and was then elevated to Senior Captain in the year of Frank Jarvis's presidency. Belgrave had been suffering a lean time in track and field and Frank made an appeal for just one major victory. Alan and the team responded by winning three trophy meetings, quite something in those pre-league days. In addition he had been a Committee member since Junior level and was co-editor of "The Belgravian" from 1961 to 1967; having been an active contributor before that. So his decision to go to Australia was a disappointment to Belgrave. In Sydney he returned to banking, but when his branch suffered a hold-up his feet itched again. A camper van was purchased and a 4 months trek ensued through and around Australia. He particularly remembers a blissful period at Cairns living on fish and coconuts, languishing in the sun and reminiscing about the Kray twins in Brixton Prison! After two years abroad he returned to England in 1971, went to Computer Training School, became a programmer and now works for Capital House, an Investment Management company. But this determination to secure a final niche for himself did not prevent a renewed involvement in Belgrave Harriers. He became the sole Editor of the ailing "Belgravian" in 1972, took over the Track Secretaryship from Bob Taylor and also the managership of the Southern League team; our first team in those days. He was also active on the social side and organised film evenings and other events. But after eight years it became too much. His aspirations required help that was no longer there, and in the early eighties he withdrew from these commitments with a feeling of disillusionment. A lover of music, particularly folk-rock, Alan turned his attention to the less frantic world of Morris dancing. He learned to play the melodeon and concertina and after three years became the lead dancer ("squire") of his team. All this time he was watching Belgrave's results and avidly reading "The Belgravian". From time to time various members would contact him in the hope he would become active again; and indeed throughout the whole period he and Pat were regular members of the results team at our 12-stage Relay events. By the late '80s he was back on Committee again and offering to help Charlie Dickinson create a "new" Belgravian magazine. Alan was keen to use desk-top publishing techniques and after discussions with Charlie they took the plunge into a new colour format. As co-editors they now produce the finest magazine in our history and probably the best club publication in the land. As usual, Alan's interest extended beyond this commitment and he was soon showing much interest in a re-structuring and a formalising of Belgrave's constitution. He was Derek Manning's principal aide in drafting the proposals and he now wishes to see the momentum maintained. He recognises that, as with most clubs, our set-up is fragile. We need to work hard at maintaining our eminent position: it is all too easy to slide down the slippery slope. He believes that a list of aims should be drawn up and the targets assessed annually. Issues of membership, young athletes from the local community, the manning of home meetings, the gymnasium and Belgrave's image are all matters close to his heart. Alan's loyalty to Belgrave is paramount, but it must not be forgotten that he is ably supported by two other Belgravians, his wife Pat and daughter Hazel. Alan and Pat met at Battersea Park and in 1966 became yet another Belgrave/Selsonia union. Hazel was born in 1977 and has been steeped in the tradition of Belgrave. They are a formidable trio. Much of their lives are devoted to the Club. All three compete for club teams and are frequently involved in the running of the meetings at the same time. We are lucky indeed to have such a family at the helm of our affairs in 1993/4. items.h: A few words from The President
items.sum: New President Alan Mead on the simple appeal of athletics and the need to bring more local young people into the club.
items.s: A few words from The President New President Alan Mead on the simple appeal of athletics and the need to bring more local young people into the club. A few words from The President Those who know me will not be surprised to hear me say that I do love athletics. I have often pondered on what it has been that has drawn me into this activity with such passion and I believe that the answer is its sheer simplicity and world-wide appeal. What could be more natural as a youngster than to try to run to the next tree faster than one's playmate; to heave a rock further than the boy down the road. Those same basic instincts are in us whether we live on an African plain, a South Sea Island or in South London. Technique and training don't come into it. We want, in the words of the Nike advert, to "Just Do It". Some of us, having enjoyed the exhuberance of "just doing it", then, "just can't stop doing it". Now it does get technical as we have to learn every trick available to do our best. In athletics there are no limits imposed by anything outside ourselves. One simply sets one's own targets and finds the level at which we are prepared to operate. For some the aim is to be the best in the world; others simply want to enjoy the continued ability to keep in touch with that early instinct. But there are always targets to attain for everyone: best under 17 in the district - furthest throw while in my fifties - a couple of sessions a week to keep the old heart ticking over. Not everyone is lucky enough to discover themselves, however. When I was about thirteen I was a youngster looking for trouble - one who just needed something on which to expend an abundance of surplus energy. I was fortunate to discover organised athletics and this Club but the story does not unfold so happily for all young people. Tree running and rock throwing do not fit easily into city life. There must be many thousands of boys and girls in our area missing out on the joy of being fit, perhaps finding themselves getting beyond the stage of mischievousness and using their energies in ways that do not bring happiness to themselves or others. We must all get out there and find them; encourage them to join us. It is difficult to think of another activity in life where one can enjoy the company of so many diverse types of people and forge friendships with them that will last for a lifetime. Differing religions mean nothing to us, nor do social backgrounds or ethnic origins. We are men and women, young and old; we have a common bond in our sport and Club; we are family. Alan Mead Alan Mead Alan Mead President South London

items.s: Club notes: walkers on TV demonstrating a lifting-detection device, Bill Couzens regaining the 'Denmark Pot' darts trophy, Belgravians dominating the Surrey Supper raffle, and the "Scrubbers and Others" Christmas eating contest. ♦ Our walkers are making a bid for the limelight. The BBC Television production 'Tomorrow's World' recently featured the invention of Canadian Dr. Dennis Furlong by which walkers who do not maintain contact with the ground are immediately and obviously identified. A small module attached to each of a competitor's shoes emits a sound and light as soon as both feet are off the ground at once. Where do our walkers come in? Well, Carl Lawton, Gill Broderick and Paul Warburton were videoed in action, demonstrating the equipment. But that's not all - they are due on 'Good Morning' with Anne and Nick some time in January. They've only got to get an invite to 'Crinkly Bottom' and they will be outdoing John Regis. ♦ After 30 years of competition for the 'Denmark Pot' the trophy has returned home to Bill Couzens. We wonder if dear old Don Maclean, sadly no longer with us, ever dreamed in 1963 that the Pot he presented would be held in such high regard for so long. Bill, for years the organiser of the event, was the winner of that very first championship held in 1963 and since then he has won the trophy more times than anyone else - but not since 1976. He was thrilled to win again but it wasn't an easy task. In the second round Tom Carter had put out Kevin Crookes, holder for the last three years, and then he stormed through the next round with a marvellous three dart finish. In the final he had Bill worried as both were together on a finishing double. Next year Tom? ♦ Belgrave made a big impact on the Surrey Supper, held at Belgrave Hall one Saturday evening in November. Marcello cooked the meal, the waitresses were Belgrave girls and it seemed that at least half the diners were from our Club. When it came to the raffle no fewer than nine of the ten prizes went to Belgravians. When that single prize not staying with us went to a Croydon Harrier there was a mighty cheer from the rest, followed by a light-hearted query from Herne Hill's John Gebbels "You're not second-claim Belgrave are you? There's more rigging in here than on the Victory!" ♦ A great night was had by a couple of dozen Belgravians at the "Scrubbers and Others" Christmas bash. Warming up was conducted in a local hostelry before the main event of the night - as much as you can eat for the set price - was started at the Mongolian Restaurant. Apart from the decor there wasn't a Mongolian in sight - all the officials seemed to be Australian! At the gun a great start was made by Keith Duckett, getting through the first course of "Yak Attack" before some had got the wine order sorted. But it was Mark Hutton who made all the running after that. For lap after lap he returned to the "help yourself bar" to select his next choice for the stir fry. Only one man could get anywhere near him in his quest to become "Gannet of the Year" - Derek Crookes. However, even Mr. Hutton has his limits and chants of "Mark - Mark - make it six" failed to get him out of his seat for more than five helpings, and Derek cruised up to end the contest in a draw. items.s: Mr. Belmore predicts 'silver' only Letter from Bob Belmore of Veterans AC and Barnet AC praising issue 220, predicting more veterans' silver medals behind Barnet, and thanking the club for use of its Hall, with a photo of him beside a 'Belgrave' station sign near Melbourne. Write on ! Mr. Belmore predicts 'silver' only Dear Editors, I was very pleased to receive "The Belgravian" no. 220. Excellent copy and one of the best club magazines I have seen; a good blend at all levels of the sport, young and old with news items, results, special features and, for me, tales of the past by Arthur Bruce. With reference to the over 60 photo' and your comments of "old friends" at the Burnley National Vet's CC Champs., I doubt if they will find the Southern Road Relay Champs. so easy this year either. Even with Laurie, the young lad who grabbed my UK 5000m record last year! Still, another set of silver medals behind Barnet again will match those won at Burnley and the Sutton Coldfield Nat. Road Relay! May I take this opportunity on behalf of Veterans AC, and personally, to thank the Club for allowing us to use their Hall in Denmark Road for cross country meetings during the winter. A special thankyou too for the Belgrave Officials who have assisted us at track and cross country - and of course those behind the bar. Naturally many of our VAC members wear the Bels colours both in our running and walking events - all are very welcome. I have enclosed a photo' taken near Melbourne on a tour in the hills during the World Vet's Championships in December 1987. As an old "2nd-claimer" I couldn't resist the name! Someone knows you out there. Bob Belmore, Veterans and Barnet AC Left: Bob Belmore might be Barnet now but only a true Belgravian would pose in front of a sign like that.
